summary: A small, apple-scented annual daisy whose hollow, domed flower heads have been steeped into one of the world's most-drunk herbal teas for over two thousand years. Its essential oil turns an inky blue when distilled, thanks to chamazulene formed from the flower's matricin.
nativeRange: Southern & Eastern Europe and Western Asia; naturalised across temperate regions worldwide
abilities: Produces apigenin and α-bisabolol, compounds studied for calming and anti-inflammatory effects
Yields a deep-blue essential oil: matricin in the flowers converts to chamazulene during steam distillation
Colonises compacted, poor and slightly saline soils such as field margins and roadsides
Completes its life cycle from seed to flower in about two months
edibilityNote: Dried flower heads are brewed as tea. People allergic to ragweed, chrysanthemums or other Asteraceae may react, occasionally severely.

uses.use: Tea for sleeplessness, nervous stomach, colic and menstrual cramps; compresses and rinses for inflamed skin and gums
Bābūnaj used as a resolvent and anti-inflammatory, in oils for joint pain and in decoctions for digestive complaints
Babuna flowers given for indigestion, flatulence and restlessness in children
Oral extracts trialled for generalised anxiety disorder; topical preparations approved in Germany for skin and mucosal inflammation

medicinal.cautions: Asteraceae allergy (including anaphylaxis in rare cases). May add to the effect of sedatives and has been reported to interact with warfarin. Avoid large medicinal doses in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Tiny, dry, pale and ribbed, without a pappus; not eaten.

seed.description: Minute pale-brown, ribbed seeds
seed.dispersal: Falls near the parent; carried by water, soil and machinery; self-sows freely
seed.germination: Needs light; surface-sow and keep moist, 7–14 days at 15–20 °C

grow.propagation: Seed, sown in spring or autumn
steps: Scatter seed on the surface of raked soil and press in lightly without covering
Keep moist until seedlings appear, then thin to about 20 cm
Pick flower heads on a dry morning when the white petals are flat or just turning back
Dry on screens out of direct sun and store airtight

lore: Dioscorides described it as anthemis in De Materia Medica (1st century CE), and bābūnaj became a fixture of medieval Arabic and Unani pharmacy. In Beatrix Potter's The Tale of Peter Rabbit (1902), Peter's mother doses him with chamomile tea.
funFact: You can tell true German chamomile from the lookalike scentless mayweed by slicing the flower head: chamomile's cone-shaped receptacle is hollow.

summary: A feathery-leaved perennial of meadows and roadsides found across most of the Northern Hemisphere, named for Achilles, who by legend used it to stop his soldiers' bleeding. Its flat-topped white flower clusters are visited by hundreds of insect species.
nativeRange: Circumboreal: Europe, temperate Asia and North America (where both native and introduced forms occur)
abilities: Contains achilleine and tannins traditionally used to slow bleeding from small wounds
Feathery, finely divided leaves ("millefolium" = thousand-leaved) reduce water loss in dry sites
Spreads by rhizomes to form drought-tolerant mats, used in lawns and erosion control
Flat-topped flower clusters (corymbs) feed a broad range of hoverflies, small bees and parasitoid wasps that control garden pests
Grows from sea level to above 3,500 m in the Rockies and Himalaya
edibilityNote: Young leaves are bitter and used in small amounts as a herb; historically used to bitter beer. Contains thujone in some chemotypes. Avoid in pregnancy. Can be confused with poisonous Apiaceae such as poison hemlock by beginners; check the leaves carefully.

uses.use: Crushed leaves on cuts and nosebleeds; tea for colds, fever and digestive complaints
Used by many nations, including the Cherokee, Ojibwe and Navajo, as a poultice for wounds and as a tea for fevers, colds and toothache
Biranjasif given as a diaphoretic and for digestive and menstrual complaints
Related Achillea species used externally for wounds, swelling and snakebite

medicinal.cautions: Asteraceae allergy and contact dermatitis. Traditionally used to bring on menstruation, so avoid in pregnancy. May increase sensitivity to sunlight.

fruit.description: Tiny, flattened, silvery-grey; not eaten.

seed.description: Flat, oblong, grey seeds without a pappus
seed.dispersal: Wind, animals and soil movement; also spreads by rhizomes

grow.soil: Any well-drained soil; thrives in poor, dry ground
grow.propagation: Seed or division in spring or autumn
grow.timeToHarvest: Flowers the second summer from seed, or the first from divisions
steps: Surface-sow in spring or plant divisions about 30 cm apart
Water until established, then leave dry; rich soil makes it floppy
Cut flowering stems when the clusters are fully open and hang to dry
Divide every few years to control spreading

lore: Pliny the Elder records that Achilles used the plant on wounds, which gave the genus its name. In China, dried yarrow stalks were the traditional tool for casting I Ching hexagrams.
funFact: The classical I Ching divination used 50 yarrow stalks, sorted by hand over and over to build each six-line hexagram.

summary: A ginger relative whose orange rhizomes colour curries, robes and wedding rituals across South Asia. Cultivated turmeric is a sterile hybrid that survives only because people have replanted its rhizomes for thousands of years.
nativeRange: Domesticated in South Asia, probably India; not known in a truly wild state. Cultivated throughout the tropics
abilities: Rhizomes contain curcuminoids, intensely yellow pigments that dye cloth and food
Curcumin is one of the most-studied plant compounds for anti-inflammatory activity
Triploid and seed-sterile; it is propagated entirely by people replanting rhizome pieces
Survives the dry season dormant underground and resprouts with the monsoon
edibleParts: leaves (used to wrap and steam food)
edibilityNote: Safe as a culinary spice. Concentrated curcumin supplements, especially those with added piperine, have been linked to rare cases of liver injury. Ground turmeric has been found adulterated with lead chromate in some markets.

uses.use: Haridra used as a blood purifier, for wounds, skin disease, cough and diabetes (prameha); applied as a paste to skin
Zard chob used externally for swelling and wounds and internally for jaundice and liver complaints
Jianghuang said to move blood and qi, for pain in the chest, abdomen and shoulders
Rhizome drinks such as Indonesian jamu kunyit asam for menstrual pain and general wellbeing

medicinal.cautions: Curcumin is poorly absorbed, and trials are mixed apart from modest effects in knee osteoarthritis. High-dose supplements may raise bleeding risk with anticoagulants, aggravate gallstones and, rarely, injure the liver. Buy from tested sources because of lead adulteration.

seed.description: Cultivated turmeric is triploid and practically never sets viable seed

grow.zones: USDA 8–12 (rhizomes lifted or protected where winters freeze)
grow.water: High during growth; dry when dormant
grow.timeToHarvest: 8–10 months, when leaves yellow and die back
steps: Plant rhizome pieces 5 cm deep in warm soil (above 20 °C) at the start of the wet season
Mulch heavily and keep evenly moist while leafing
Harvest when the foliage dies back; keep some rhizomes for replanting
Boil, sun-dry and grind the rest for spice

lore: Turmeric paste is applied to the bride and groom at the Hindu haldi ceremony before a wedding. The saffron-yellow robes of Theravada Buddhist monks were traditionally dyed with turmeric or jackfruit heartwood.
funFact: A 2019 Stanford-led study found that some turmeric in Bangladesh had been brightened with lead chromate, a toxic industrial pigment. It was traced as a likely source of lead in people's blood.

summary: A grey-velvety nightshade-family shrub of dry country, whose horse-scented roots are Ayurveda's best-known rasayana (rejuvenating tonic). Its small orange-red berries hide inside papery lanterns, like those of its cousin the Chinese lantern.
nativeRange: Dry regions from the Mediterranean and North & East Africa through the Middle East to India and Sri Lanka
abilities: Makes withanolides, steroidal lactones such as withaferin A that are studied for anti-inflammatory and anti-stress activity
Tolerates drought, heat and poor alkaline soils, needing very little water
Encloses its berries in an inflated papery calyx that protects them as they ripen
edibilityNote: Roots are taken as a powder or extract, not eaten as food. Like many Solanaceae, leaves and unripe berries contain potentially toxic compounds.

uses.use: Rasayana tonic for debility, ageing, insomnia, stress and low libido; given in milk (ashwagandha ksheerapaka)
Asgandh used as a nervine and aphrodisiac tonic and applied to painful swellings
Leaves and roots used in parts of East and Southern Africa as poultices for wounds and for fever
Root extracts trialled for stress, anxiety and sleep, with small positive studies

medicinal.cautions: Liver injury has been reported with supplements, and Denmark banned ashwagandha products in 2023. May raise thyroid hormone levels and add to sedatives. Avoid in pregnancy, as it was traditionally used to cause abortion, and take care with autoimmune disease or immunosuppressants. Trials are mostly small and short.

fruit.description: Orange-red berry about 6 mm wide, enclosed in a papery husk; not eaten.

seed.description: Flat, kidney-shaped, yellowish seeds

grow.soil: Sandy or stony, well-drained, slightly alkaline
steps: Sow seed shallowly in warm soil in late spring or at the start of the rains
Thin seedlings to 30–60 cm and water sparingly
Harvest roots when the berries ripen and the leaves begin to dry
Wash, cut and sun-dry the roots

lore: The Charaka Samhita (c. 1st–2nd century CE) lists ashwagandha among the strengthening herbs. Its Sanskrit name, 'smell of horse', is said to describe both the root's odour and the strength it was believed to give.
funFact: Linnaeus first placed the plant in the genus Physalis, alongside tomatillos and Cape gooseberries, because of the lantern-like husk around its berry.

summary: A fast-growing, drought-hardy evergreen of the Indian subcontinent, known in Sanskrit as sarva roga nivarini, 'healer of all ailments'. Its seeds yield azadirachtin, one of the most powerful natural insect deterrents known.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent and drier parts of mainland Southeast Asia; widely planted across Africa, the Middle East, Australia and the Americas
abilities: Seeds contain azadirachtin, which stops many insects feeding and disrupts their moulting, at very low doses
Survives on as little as 400–1,200 mm of rain a year and puts down a deep taproot
Grows quickly on degraded, stony and alkaline soils; widely planted to hold back the Sahel
Stays in leaf through the dry season and casts dense shade
edibilityNote: Tender leaves and flowers are eaten in small amounts in South Asian dishes, such as Bengali neem-begun and the Ugadi pachadi of South India. Neem seed oil is toxic if swallowed and has caused fatal encephalopathy and liver failure in infants. Never give neem oil by mouth.

uses.use: Bitter leaves and bark for skin diseases, fever, intestinal worms and blood purification; twigs used as a chewing stick (datun) for teeth
Leaves and bark used as a blood purifier and antiseptic for boils, eczema and wounds
Dogonyaro leaf and bark decoctions widely used against fever and malaria
Leaf paste and oil applied for skin infections, smallpox and chickenpox care

medicinal.cautions: Seed oil is poisonous by mouth, especially to children, and can cause vomiting, seizures, metabolic acidosis and death. Leaf extracts have antifertility effects in animals, so avoid during pregnancy or when trying to conceive. Not proven to treat malaria.

fruit.season: Early to mid summer (June–August in India)
fruit.description: Olive-like, 1.5–2 cm, ripening yellow with thin sweetish pulp around one hard seed.

seed.description: Single oily kernel inside a hard shell
seed.dispersal: Birds and bats eat the fruit
seed.germination: Fresh seed only, as viability falls within weeks; 1–3 weeks at 25–35 °C

grow.soil: Any well-drained soil; tolerates poor, stony and alkaline ground; dislikes waterlogging
grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves within a year; fruit from 3–5 years
steps: Sow freshly cleaned seed within days of collection
Transplant seedlings at 3–4 months into a sunny, frost-free site
Water through the first dry season only
Prune to shape, as it tolerates heavy lopping

lore: Neem is worshipped in many Indian villages as an embodiment of the goddess Shitala or Mariamman, and its leaves are hung over doorways at Gudi Padwa and Ugadi. The Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita both prescribe nimba for skin disease.
funFact: In 2000 the European Patent Office revoked a patent on a neem-based fungicide, finding that its use had long been known in India. The case became a landmark in fights over 'biopiracy'.

summary: A clove-scented basil that grows in a raised shrine (tulsi vrindavan) in the courtyard of countless Hindu homes, where it is worshipped as the goddess Tulsi. It is also the peppery basil of Thai street food.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent to Southeast Asia and northern Australia
abilities: Leaves are rich in eugenol, the clove-scented compound that deters many insects
Flowers almost year-round in the tropics and feeds bees and other small pollinators
Contains ursolic and rosmarinic acids, studied for anti-inflammatory activity
edibilityNote: Leaves are used fresh in Thai cooking (pad kraphao) and in teas. Medicinal amounts are best avoided in pregnancy.

uses.use: Leaf tea and juice for cough, colds, fever and stress; used as a rasayana and to support breathing
Thulasi leaves given for respiratory infections and as a general tonic
Leaf infusions in Thailand for stomach ache, colic and colds
Small trials of extracts for stress, blood sugar and lipids

medicinal.cautions: Clinical trials are few, small and of mixed quality. May lower blood sugar and slow clotting. Animal studies suggest reduced fertility, so avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy or when trying to conceive. Methyl eugenol in the essential oil is a concern at high doses.

fruit.season: Most of the year in the tropics
fruit.description: Tiny dry nutlets held in the persistent calyx.

seed.description: Small brown-black seeds that turn mucilaginous when wet

steps: Sow on the surface of warm compost and keep moist
Plant out after frost into full sun
Pinch out tips to keep it bushy
Harvest leaves often; let some flower for bees and seed

lore: In the Puranas Tulsi is the consort of Vishnu, and the annual Tulsi Vivah festival ritually marries the plant to Vishnu as the shaligram stone or to Krishna. Vaishnava devotees wear prayer beads (kanthi mala) carved from tulsi stems.
funFact: Much medical literature still calls holy basil Ocimum sanctum. But Linnaeus had already named it O. tenuiflorum in 1753, fourteen years earlier, so that name takes priority.

summary: A towering biennial of woodland clearings whose spotted purple bells are built for bumblebees, and whose leaves gave medicine one of its most important heart drugs. Every part is poisonous; the gap between a healing dose and a deadly one is very small.
nativeRange: Western and south-western Europe and north-western Africa; naturalised in North America, New Zealand and elsewhere
abilities: Makes cardiac glycosides such as digitoxin that strengthen and slow the heartbeat
Spotted flower tubes act as landing guides for bumblebees, its main pollinators
A single plant sheds vast numbers of dust-like seeds that persist for years in the soil
Springs up quickly after woodland is felled or burned
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous. Before flowering its leaf rosettes have been mistaken for comfrey or borage, with fatal results. Children and pets are at risk.

uses.use: Leaf preparations for dropsy (oedema), recorded by William Withering from a Shropshire family remedy
Source of digitoxin, used for heart failure and atrial fibrillation; the related D. lanata yields digoxin

medicinal.cautions: Deadly poisonous. Symptoms include vomiting, yellow-green vision, dangerous heart rhythms and death. The isolated glycosides are prescription drugs with a narrow safety margin. Never self-medicate with the plant.

fruit.description: Egg-shaped dry capsule splitting in two to release seed; poisonous.

seed.description: Minute reddish-brown seeds
seed.dispersal: Shaken from capsules by wind; persistent soil seed bank

grow.timeToHarvest: Flowers in its second year (ornamental only)
steps: Surface-sow in late spring or summer
Plant rosettes out in autumn, away from children's play areas and edible beds
Let it flower the next summer and self-seed
Wear gloves when handling

lore: In 1785 William Withering, a Birmingham physician, published An Account of the Foxglove, describing ten years of careful dose trials for dropsy. It is a founding text of clinical pharmacology.
funFact: The name Digitalis comes from Leonhart Fuchs, who in 1542 Latinised the German Fingerhut, 'thimble', as digitalis.

summary: A tall riverside tree whose leaves flash silver in the wind and whose bark held the salicylates that led chemists to aspirin. Its catkins are among the first spring food for bees.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western & Central Asia; widely planted and naturalised elsewhere
abilities: Bark contains salicin, which the body converts to salicylic acid, a pain-relieving and anti-inflammatory compound
Roots readily from cut stems; a branch pushed into wet ground can become a tree
Binds riverbanks with dense roots and tolerates long floods
Catkins, opening with the leaves in spring, give early pollen and nectar to bees
edibilityNote: Bark is used as a medicinal tea or extract, not as food. People allergic to aspirin should avoid it.

uses.use: Bark decoction for fevers ('agues'), rheumatism and pain
Leaves and bark of bed used for fevers, inflammation and as a cooling astringent
Standardised bark extracts for low back pain and osteoarthritis

medicinal.cautions: Avoid with aspirin or salicylate allergy, asthma triggered by aspirin, anticoagulant therapy, stomach ulcers, and in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Not for children with viral illness because of the theoretical risk of Reye's syndrome.

fruit.description: Small capsules on female catkins, splitting to release cottony seeds.

seed.description: Tiny seeds wrapped in silky white hairs
seed.germination: Short-lived (days); must land on wet bare mud to germinate within 24–48 h

steps: Push 30–50 cm dormant cuttings into moist soil in late winter
Keep well watered the first summer
Plant at least 15 m from drains and buildings, as the roots are aggressive
Coppice or pollard every few years for bark and withies

lore: In 1763 the Rev. Edward Stone reported to the Royal Society that powdered willow bark cured agues in 50 patients. Salicylic acid chemistry later led Felix Hoffmann at Bayer to acetylsalicylic acid, sold as Aspirin from 1899.
funFact: Cricket bats are made from a variety of this tree, the cricket-bat willow, Salix alba var. caerulea.

summary: A prairie daisy with drooping magenta petals around a spiny copper cone, now one of the best-selling herbal medicines in the world. The genus name comes from the Greek echinos, hedgehog, after that prickly cone.
nativeRange: Eastern and central United States: open woods and prairies from Ohio and Michigan south to Louisiana and Georgia
abilities: Roots contain alkamides that cause a tingling numbness on the tongue
Long-lasting flowers feed bees and butterflies, and seed heads feed goldfinches into winter
Deep taproots and fibrous roots let it survive prairie droughts and fires
edibilityNote: Used as tea, tincture or extract rather than as food.

uses.use: Plains nations used Echinacea, mainly E. angustifolia and E. pallida, for toothache, sore throat, snakebite and wounds; E. purpurea itself was less used
Popularised from the 1880s by Eclectic physicians and the Lloyd Brothers for infections and 'bad blood'
Aerial-part and root extracts taken to prevent or shorten colds; pressed juice approved in Germany

medicinal.cautions: Trials are inconsistent: some show a small effect on preventing colds, few show it shortens them. Asteraceae allergy, including rare anaphylaxis, and rashes in children. Theoretically unsuitable with autoimmune disease or immunosuppressant drugs.

fruit.description: Four-angled, tan achenes in the spiny cone; eaten by birds, not people.

seed.description: Angular, tan, crowned with tiny teeth
seed.dispersal: Falls near the parent; birds scatter some
seed.germination: Improved by 4–6 weeks' cold moist stratification; 10–20 days at 20 °C

grow.soil: Well-drained loam; tolerates clay and drought
grow.timeToHarvest: Flowers in year 1–2; roots at 3–4 years
steps: Sow outdoors in autumn or stratify seed in the fridge before spring sowing
Plant 45 cm apart in sun
Leave seed heads standing for birds over winter
Divide clumps every 4 years

lore: In the 1880s the Nebraska patent-medicine maker H. C. F. Meyer sold 'Meyer's Blood Purifier' made from Echinacea. In the 1930s the German firm Madaus mistakenly imported E. purpurea seed instead of E. angustifolia, and so built Europe's echinacea industry on this species.
funFact: Linnaeus first classed it as a Rudbeckia, a black-eyed Susan. It was moved to its own genus, Echinacea, by Conrad Moench in 1794.

summary: A slow-growing forest herb whose forked, human-shaped root has been the most prized tonic of East Asian medicine for two thousand years. Wild roots have been dug almost to extinction, and old specimens fetch extraordinary prices.
nativeRange: Mixed and broadleaf forests of north-eastern China, the Korean Peninsula and the Russian Far East; now almost entirely cultivated
abilities: Makes ginsenosides, triterpene saponins studied for effects on fatigue, immunity and blood sugar
Can live for decades, adding one stem scar to the root neck each year
Seeds have a double dormancy and take about 18–22 months to germinate
Needs deep forest shade; leaves scorch in full sun
edibilityNote: Eaten in Korean dishes such as samgyetang (ginseng chicken soup) and taken as tea or extract. Large or long-term doses can cause insomnia, raised blood pressure and nervousness.

uses.use: Renshen strongly tonifies yuan qi; used for exhaustion, shortness of breath, collapse and as a superior longevity herb
Steamed red ginseng (hongsam) used as a daily restorative and for fatigue and immunity
Extracts trialled for fatigue, cognition, erectile dysfunction and blood sugar control

medicinal.cautions: May reduce warfarin's effect, lower blood sugar and interact with MAOIs and stimulants. Can cause insomnia, headache and high blood pressure. Not recommended in pregnancy. Buy cultivated roots; the wild plant is critically endangered.

fruit.description: Bright red, two-seeded berries in a single round cluster above the leaves.

seed.description: Cream-white, flattened, wrinkled seeds
seed.germination: Needs warm then cold stratification over 18–22 months; usually sold pre-stratified

grow.soil: Loose, humus-rich forest loam, slightly acidic
steps: Plant stratified seed 2 cm deep in autumn under a hardwood canopy or 70–80% shade cloth
Mulch with leaf litter and keep weeds down
Watch for slugs and fungal rots in wet years
Dig carefully in autumn of year 4–6, keeping the fine root hairs intact

lore: The Shennong Bencao Jing (c. 1st–2nd century CE) ranks ginseng among the 'superior' herbs that nourish life. In 1716 the Jesuit Joseph-François Lafitau found its relative, American ginseng, near Montreal after reading a colleague's description of the Chinese plant, and started a transpacific root trade.
funFact: Panax comes from the Greek panakeia, 'all-healing', the same root as panacea.

summary: A tall, damp-meadow perennial with sweetly scented pink-white flowers above roots that smell powerfully of old socks. Those roots have been Europe's classic sleep remedy since Galen's day, and cats find them irresistible.
nativeRange: Europe and temperate Asia; naturalised in North America
abilities: Roots produce valerenic acid and valepotriates, which act on GABA-A receptors in lab studies
Root odour comes from isovaleric acid, which forms as the roots dry
Attracts cats, which roll on the roots much as they do on catnip
Fragrant flower heads draw hoverflies, bees and butterflies
edibilityNote: Root is used as tea, tincture or capsules, not as food.

uses.use: Root tea for insomnia, nervous tension, palpitations and cramps; Galen prescribed 'phu' for insomnia
Root extracts approved in Germany and by the EMA (traditional use) for mild nervous tension and sleep disorders
Related valerians (asaroon, sumbul-ut-teeb) used as nervines; V. officinalis root used similarly in Persian pharmacy

medicinal.cautions: Sleep trials are inconsistent and effects modest at best. Can cause drowsiness, headache and morning grogginess, and adds to alcohol and sedative drugs, so do not drive after taking it. Rare cases of liver injury. Not advised in pregnancy or for young children.

fruit.description: Small one-seeded fruit crowned with a parachute of plumes.

seed.description: Oblong, ribbed seed with a feathery pappus
seed.germination: Needs light; 2–3 weeks at 18–20 °C; viability falls after a year

steps: Surface-sow fresh seed in spring
Plant 45–60 cm apart in moist soil
Remove flower stems in year 2 to send energy into the roots
Lift roots in autumn, wash quickly and dry at under 40 °C

lore: Dioscorides and Galen called it phu, a word thought to echo disgust at its smell. It is reported to have been used in Britain during the World Wars for nervous strain, including the stress of air raids.
funFact: Cats react to valerian root because of actinidine, a compound related to the nepetalactone in catnip.

otherNames: Guàn yè lián qiáo 贯叶连翘 (Chinese)
summary: A golden-flowered meadow perennial that blooms around midsummer, St John's Day. Its leaves are pricked with translucent oil glands and its flowers bleed red. It works as an antidepressant, but also speeds up the liver's clearance of many prescription drugs.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western & Central Asia; invasive in North America, Australia and elsewhere
abilities: Extracts containing hyperforin and hypericin outperform placebo for mild to moderate depression in clinical trials
Translucent leaf glands make the leaves look perforated when held to the light
Flowers stain the fingers and oils red with hypericin
Hypericin is photodynamic: grazing animals that eat it can suffer severe sunburn (hypericism)
Spreads aggressively by seed and runners; a major rangeland weed outside its native range
edibilityNote: Not a food. Toxic to livestock, which become photosensitised. In people it is taken only as standardised medicine.

uses.use: Red flower oil for wounds, burns and nerve pain; tea for melancholy and bedwetting
Hufariqun used as a diuretic, wound-healer and for sciatica
Standardised extracts prescribed in Germany for mild to moderate depression

medicinal.cautions: Systematic reviews find it better than placebo and similar to standard antidepressants for mild to moderate depression. It strongly induces CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, which can make oral contraceptives, warfarin, ciclosporin, HIV drugs, digoxin, some chemotherapy and many other drugs fail. Do not combine with SSRIs or other serotonergic drugs, as serotonin syndrome can result. Causes photosensitivity. Seek medical advice before using it for depression.

fruit.description: Three-chambered dry capsule with many seeds.

seed.description: Tiny, cylindrical, dark brown, finely pitted
seed.dispersal: Wind, water, animals and machinery; long-lived seed bank

steps: Check local rules first: it is a declared noxious weed in many US states, Australia and elsewhere
Surface-sow in spring
Harvest the top third of flowering stems at peak bloom
Macerate fresh flowers in olive oil in sun for 'red oil', or dry quickly for tea

lore: Medieval Europeans hung it over doors on St John's Eve (23 June) to repel evil spirits, and it was known as fuga daemonum, 'devil's flight'. Dioscorides and Pliny recommended hyperikon for sciatica and burns.
funFact: In the 1940s California released Chrysolina leaf beetles against Klamath weed, as St John's wort was called there. It became one of the first great successes of biological weed control.

summary: A cheerful orange-and-gold daisy of cottage gardens whose resinous petals colour soups and soothe skin. It is not the Tagetes 'marigold' of Indian garlands, though the two are often confused.
nativeRange: Known only in cultivation; probably derived from Mediterranean Calendula species. Grown worldwide
abilities: Petals contain carotenoids (lutein, lycopene) that dye food and fabric yellow-orange
Triterpenoid faradiol esters show anti-inflammatory activity on skin
One plant bears several very different seed shapes (heterocarpy), spreading its bets on dispersal
Flowers open in sunshine and close in dull weather
edibilityNote: Petals colour rice, cheese and butter and garnish salads. Do not confuse it with Tagetes marigolds or the poisonous marsh marigold (Caltha). People allergic to Asteraceae may react.

uses.use: Ointments and infused oils for cuts, burns, nappy rash and sore nipples; petal tea for digestion and menstrual pain
Flowers used as a resolvent for swellings and for liver and menstrual complaints
Topical creams studied for radiation dermatitis, leg ulcers and episiotomy healing; EMA traditional-use monograph for minor skin inflammation

medicinal.cautions: Asteraceae allergy and contact dermatitis. Trials for radiation dermatitis are conflicting. Avoid medicinal oral doses in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Curved, hooked and ridged achenes of several shapes on the same head.

seed.description: C-shaped, knobbly, beige-brown seeds of several forms
seed.dispersal: Hooked forms catch on fur; others fall or blow
seed.germination: Easy; 5–14 days at 15–21 °C; cover with 1 cm soil (needs darkness)

steps: Sow directly 1 cm deep in spring or autumn
Thin to 25–30 cm
Pick flowers every few days to keep new ones coming
Dry petals in shade for tea, oils or colouring

lore: Nicholas Culpeper's Complete Herbal (1653) prized marigold flowers for 'comforting the heart'. Medieval cooks used the petals as a cheap stand-in for saffron.
funFact: Its name comes from the Latin calendae, the first day of the month, because in mild climates it seemed to be in flower at the start of every month.

summary: A stemless succulent whose plump leaves hold a cool, clear gel under a yellow, bitter latex, two quite different medicines in one leaf. It is grown on every continent but no longer known in the wild.
nativeRange: Probably originated in the Arabian Peninsula; known only in cultivation. Naturalised in arid regions worldwide
abilities: Uses CAM photosynthesis, opening its pores only at night to save water
Leaf gel is mostly water bound in polysaccharides such as acemannan
Yellow latex under the skin contains aloin, a strong purgative
Survives months of drought by drawing on water stored in its leaves
edibilityNote: The clear inner gel is eaten and drunk, for example in Asian aloe drinks, once the yellow latex has been rinsed off completely. The latex (aloin) is a harsh laxative and can cause cramping, diarrhoea and potassium loss.

uses.use: Ghritakumari gel for burns, skin disease, liver disorders and as a female tonic (kumari asava)
Dried latex (sibr/musabbar) as a purgative and in pills for liver and skin complaints
Luhui (dried latex) used to purge heat and for constipation and worms
Topical gel for minor burns, psoriasis and radiation skin reactions

medicinal.cautions: Topical gel for burns has modest, mixed support. In 2002 the US FDA removed aloe latex from over-the-counter laxatives for lack of safety data, and whole-leaf extract caused intestinal tumours in rats. Oral latex can cause severe diarrhoea, low potassium and kidney injury, and should be avoided in pregnancy and with digoxin or diuretics.

fruit.description: Dry three-valved capsule; seldom sets seed in cultivation.

seed.description: Flat, black, winged seeds (rarely produced)

steps: Pot offsets in cactus mix and wait a week before watering
Water deeply only when the soil is dry; much less in winter
Cut outer leaves at the base and stand upright to drain the yellow latex
Bring indoors below about 5 °C

lore: Dioscorides described aloe for wounds and purging in the 1st century CE, and dried aloe latex was traded from the Red Sea to India and China. In Arabic, sabr means both 'aloe' and 'patience'.
funFact: Barbados was long a leading exporter of dried aloe latex, sold as 'Barbados aloes', which is why the plant was once called Aloe barbadensis.

summary: A silver-leaved Mediterranean mountain shrub whose purple spikes have perfumed linen, baths and soap since Roman times. Despite its common name it is not English, and its finest oil comes from the high Provençal plateaus.
nativeRange: Mountains of the western Mediterranean: Spain, southern France, Andorra and Italy
abilities: Essential oil is dominated by linalool and linalyl acetate, studied for anxiety-reducing effects
Thrives on dry, stony, alkaline soil where few crops will grow
Silvery hairs reflect sunlight and reduce water loss
One of the most visited garden plants for bumblebees and honeybees
edibilityNote: Flowers flavour shortbread, honey and herbes de Provence in small amounts. The essential oil is toxic if swallowed in quantity.

uses.use: Flower tea, pillows and oil for sleeplessness, headaches, nervous indigestion and insect bites
Lavender species (khuzama, ustukhuddus) used as nervines to 'cleanse the brain', for headache and epilepsy
Oral lavender-oil capsules (Silexan) trialled with positive results for generalised anxiety; aromatherapy for sleep

medicinal.cautions: Essential oil can cause contact dermatitis and is poisonous if swallowed undiluted. Oral capsules can cause belching and nausea. Topical lavender and tea-tree products have been linked to breast enlargement in boys, though this is debated. May add to sedatives.

fruit.description: Four tiny dark nutlets inside each dried calyx.

seed.description: Small, oval, glossy dark brown
seed.germination: Slow and erratic; 3–4 weeks cold stratification helps; 2–4 weeks at 15–20 °C

grow.soil: Poor, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline
grow.propagation: Semi-ripe cuttings (true to type) or seed
steps: Root 8–10 cm summer cuttings in gritty compost
Plant in full sun with excellent drainage; wet winter soil kills it
Harvest stems as the first flowers open
Trim back after flowering, but never cut into old bare wood

lore: Hildegard of Bingen (12th century) wrote that lavender kept away lice and cleared the vision. The perfumer-chemist René-Maurice Gattefossé popularised the word aromathérapie with his 1937 book of that name, partly after treating a laboratory burn with lavender oil.
funFact: Lavender oil is not one product: oil from L. angustifolia is low in camphor, while hybrid lavandin (L. × intermedia) gives much more oil with a harsher, camphoraceous smell.

summary: A natural hybrid of water mint and spearmint, almost sterile and spread around the world entirely by runners. Its menthol tricks nerve endings into feeling cold.
nativeRange: Arose as a hybrid in Europe; cultivated and naturalised worldwide
abilities: Menthol activates TRPM8, the body's cold receptor, causing a cooling sensation without any change in temperature
Relaxes smooth muscle in the gut, which underlies its use for irritable bowel syndrome
Spreads rapidly by underground and overground runners
Rarely sets viable seed; almost every peppermint plant is a clone
edibilityNote: Leaves are used in teas, sweets and food. Concentrated oil is toxic in large amounts, and menthol products should not be applied near the faces of infants, where they can cause breathing problems.

uses.use: Tea for indigestion, nausea, colic and colds; oil rubbed on temples for headache
Pudina and its distilled water (araq-e-pudina) for indigestion, flatulence and vomiting
Bohe (mainly Mentha haplocalyx) disperses wind-heat in colds, sore throat and headache
Enteric-coated peppermint oil for irritable bowel syndrome; topical menthol for tension headache

medicinal.cautions: Can worsen heartburn and reflux by relaxing the oesophageal sphincter. The oil is toxic if swallowed in quantity. Keep menthol away from infants' faces. Enteric-coated capsules can interact with antacids.

fruit.description: Usually aborted; viable nutlets very rare.

seed.description: Seeds are rarely viable; 'peppermint seed' sold commercially usually grows into other mints

grow.propagation: Runner or stem cuttings (roots in water within days)
steps: Root a stem cutting in water, or plant a runner
Grow in a sunk container to stop it spreading
Cut stems just before flowering for the strongest oil
Replant every 3–4 years as clumps weaken

lore: The naturalist John Ray first described 'pepper-mint' in 1696 from a plant found in Hertfordshire. Commercial growing began at Mitcham, Surrey, in the mid-18th century.
funFact: Peppermint's chromosome counts are irregular (from 66 to 120 have been recorded), a legacy of its hybrid origin from water mint and spearmint, which is why it almost never sets viable seed.

otherNames: Shēngjiāng 生姜 / Gānjiāng 干姜 (Chinese)
summary: A reed-like tropical herb whose knobbly, pungent rhizome was one of the first spices traded from Asia to the Roman world. It is not known in the wild, and has been carried around the world by people.
nativeRange: Domesticated in Island Southeast Asia or southern China; unknown in the wild. Cultivated throughout the tropics
abilities: Gingerols in the fresh rhizome turn into hotter shogaols when dried or cooked
Acts against nausea, probably through serotonin (5-HT3) receptors in the gut
Rarely sets seed; spread worldwide entirely by rhizome cuttings
edibilityNote: Widely eaten. Large doses can cause heartburn.

uses.use: Shunthi to kindle digestive fire (agni), for nausea, colds, joint pain and as a carrier in many formulas
Fresh ginger (shengjiang) to induce sweating in colds and stop vomiting; dried ginger (ganjiang) to warm the interior
Zanjabil as a digestive and carminative, for phlegm, and as an aphrodisiac
Powdered rhizome for pregnancy nausea, motion sickness and post-operative and chemotherapy nausea

medicinal.cautions: Reasonable trial support for pregnancy nausea, much weaker for other uses. High doses may increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants, worsen gallstones and cause heartburn. In pregnancy keep to the doses used in trials, about 1 g a day.

seed.description: Seed is very rarely produced in cultivation

grow.timeToHarvest: Young ginger at 4–5 months; mature at 8–10 months
steps: Soak a fresh organic rhizome overnight and cut into pieces each with a bud
Plant 5 cm deep in warm compost, buds up
Keep warm (above 20 °C) and moist in dappled shade
Harvest when leaves yellow, or dig 'baby ginger' earlier

lore: The Analects record that Confucius 'was never without ginger when he ate'. Zanjabil is named in the Qur'an (76:17) as a flavouring of the drink of paradise.
funFact: Ginger's name has travelled through Sanskrit śṛṅgavera ('horn-shaped'), Greek zingiberis and Latin zingiber to English.

summary: A bulb so long domesticated that most varieties no longer set seed, propagated clove by clove for over five thousand years. Its sharp smell forms only when the cells are crushed, as a chemical defence.
nativeRange: Derived from wild Allium in Central Asia (Tian Shan region); known only in cultivation
abilities: Crushing mixes alliin with the enzyme alliinase to make allicin, a pungent antimicrobial defence compound
Most cultivars are sterile, making tiny bulbils in the flower head instead of seed
Needs a winter chill to divide into cloves
edibilityNote: Widely eaten. Toxic to dogs and cats, causing anaemia. Garlic stored in oil at room temperature can grow botulism bacteria.

uses.use: Lashuna as a rasayana for heart, joints, cough and worms; the Bower Manuscript opens with its praise
Thum used for chest complaints, as an antidote to poisons, and as an aphrodisiac
Dasuan to kill parasites, treat dysentery and reduce swellings
Raw cloves and syrups for colds, infections and 'thinning the blood'

medicinal.cautions: Meta-analyses show modest falls in blood pressure and cholesterol. High intake increases bleeding risk with anticoagulants and before surgery, and lowers blood levels of some HIV drugs such as saquinavir. Raw garlic on the skin can cause chemical burns.

seed.description: Most cultivars do not produce true seed; flower heads carry bulbils
seed.dispersal: Human propagation of cloves and bulbils

steps: Plant cloves pointed end up, 5 cm deep and 15 cm apart, in autumn
Mulch over winter and weed in spring
Snap off flower scapes of hardneck types to grow larger bulbs
Lift when the lower third of the leaves have browned; cure in an airy place for 2–3 weeks

lore: Herodotus wrote that an inscription on the Great Pyramid recorded the radishes, onions and garlic given to the builders. The Bower Manuscript, a Sanskrit medical collection of the late 5th or early 6th century CE found near Kucha, opens with a treatise on garlic that tells the legend of its origin.
funFact: Medieval Europeans called garlic 'the poor man's treacle', from theriac, the costly universal antidote.

summary: A bitter, strongly scented little daisy whose name is a corruption of 'febrifuge'. Today it is best known as a herbal migraine preventative.
nativeRange: Balkan Peninsula, Anatolia and the Caucasus; naturalised widely in Europe, the Americas and Australasia
abilities: Leaves contain parthenolide, a sesquiterpene lactone that blocks NF-κB inflammatory signalling in lab studies
Pungent camphor-scented foliage repels many insects
Self-seeds freely into wall crevices and paving
edibilityNote: Very bitter; chewing fresh leaves causes mouth ulcers in some people.

uses.use: Leaves eaten in bread or as tea for headache, fevers, arthritis and to bring on menstruation
Dried leaf or CO2 extract to prevent migraine attacks; EMA traditional-use monograph
Infusions used in Mexico and Central America for colic, stomach ache and menstrual pain

medicinal.cautions: Trials for migraine prevention are mixed; a Cochrane review found any benefit small and uncertain. Causes mouth ulcers and digestive upset, and stopping suddenly may cause rebound headaches ('post-feverfew syndrome'). Avoid in pregnancy because it stimulates the uterus, and with anticoagulants or Asteraceae allergy.

fruit.description: Tiny ribbed achenes with a short crown.

seed.description: Minute ribbed seeds

grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves from 3–4 months; flowers first summer
steps: Surface-sow in spring
Plant 30 cm apart in sun
Pick leaves as needed and dry for capsules or tea
Deadhead to limit self-seeding

lore: Dioscorides recommended parthenion, a name later linked to the Parthenon. The modern migraine interest began in the 1970s with Welsh patients' reports and led to a 1985 trial at the London Migraine Clinic published in the BMJ.
funFact: 'Feverfew' comes from the Latin febrifugia, 'fever-chaser', although the plant does little to lower fevers.

summary: A big, bristly riverside perennial whose roots were once packed around broken limbs to set like plaster. It works well on bruises and sprains, but contains alkaloids that harm the liver when taken by mouth.
nativeRange: Europe to Western Asia; naturalised in North America and elsewhere
abilities: Leaves and roots contain allantoin, which promotes cell proliferation in wound healing
Thick, mucilaginous roots once set hard enough to splint fractures
Deep roots draw up potassium, making its leaves a prized garden fertiliser
Bell flowers are a staple of bumblebees; short-tongued bees 'rob' nectar by biting holes in them
edibilityNote: Formerly eaten as a vegetable and tea, but all parts, especially the roots, contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids that cause liver damage. Before flowering its leaves can be mistaken for deadly foxglove.

uses.use: Root and leaf poultices for fractures, sprains, bruises and wounds; formerly teas for coughs and ulcers
Alkaloid-reduced root creams for ankle sprains, back pain and knee osteoarthritis, with positive trials

medicinal.cautions: Never take by mouth: its pyrrolizidine alkaloids can cause veno-occlusive liver disease, and in 2001 the FDA advised removing oral comfrey products from the US market. Use topically on unbroken skin only, for a limited time, preferably as alkaloid-reduced products. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

fruit.description: Shiny dark nutlets with an oil-rich attachment that ants carry off.

seed.description: Glossy black nutlets
seed.germination: Slow and erratic; root cuttings are easier

grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves from year 1; cut 3–4 times a season
steps: Plant root sections 5 cm deep where it can stay; any root fragment left behind will regrow
Keep moist the first season
Cut leaves for compost or liquid fertiliser before flowering
Label clearly and keep away from edible greens and foxgloves

lore: The name Symphytum comes from the Greek symphyo, 'to grow together', and 'comfrey' from the Latin confervere, 'to boil together' or heal. Its old English name knitbone records its traditional use on fractures.
funFact: Organic gardeners grow sterile 'Bocking 14', a Russian comfrey (S. × uplandicum) bred by Lawrence Hills, as a fertiliser plant that cannot seed itself about.

summary: A fast-growing hedgerow shrub with plates of creamy, muscat-scented flowers in early summer and drooping clusters of purple-black berries in autumn. It has been called the medicine chest of the countryside.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western Asia; naturalised elsewhere
abilities: Berries are rich in anthocyanins, which inhibit influenza viruses in laboratory studies
Thrives on nitrogen-rich ground around rabbit warrens, farmyards and middens
Soft white pith is easily pushed out of stems, leaving hollow tubes
Fruit is a major autumn food for thrushes, blackcaps and warblers fattening up for migration
edibilityNote: Flowers and fully ripe, cooked berries are used in cordials, wine, syrups and jams. Raw or unripe berries, seeds, leaves, stems, bark and roots contain cyanogenic glycosides and can cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Remove all stalks.

uses.use: Hot elderflower tea to bring on sweating in colds and fevers; berry syrup for coughs and flu; bark as a purgative
Khaman flowers and leaves used as a diaphoretic and diuretic and in poultices for swellings
Standardised berry extracts studied for shortening influenza and colds; EMA traditional-use monograph for elderflower in colds

medicinal.cautions: A handful of small trials suggest it shortens flu and colds; the evidence is limited. Raw plant parts are poisonous, so cook berries and avoid leaves, bark and seeds. May interact with diuretics and immunosuppressants.

fruit.description: Small purple-black drupes, 5–6 mm, in drooping flat clusters; each with 3–5 seeds.

seed.description: Small, wrinkled, light-brown pyrenes
seed.germination: Slow; needs warm then cold stratification, often 2 seasons

grow.soil: Fertile, moist; tolerates chalk and clay
grow.propagation: Hardwood cuttings in winter (easiest) or seed
steps: Push 25 cm hardwood cuttings into the ground in winter
Water through the first summer
Pick flower heads on a dry sunny morning, leaving some for berries
Prune out old stems each winter to keep it productive

lore: John Evelyn wrote in Sylva (1664) that if the virtues of elder were fully known, no Englishman would ail anything. Scandinavian and English folklore held that an Elder Mother lived in the tree and that wood should not be cut without asking her leave.
funFact: The name Sambucus is thought to come from the sambuca, an ancient instrument, because elder's hollow stems were made into pipes and whistles.

otherNames: Gāncǎo 甘草 (Chinese, applied to G. uralensis and G. glabra)
summary: A legume whose long yellow roots contain glycyrrhizin, a compound 30–50 times sweeter than sugar. It is so widely used in medicine that Chinese tradition calls it 'the great harmoniser' of formulas, but too much raises blood pressure dangerously.
nativeRange: Mediterranean and North Africa through Western & Central Asia to Xinjiang and northern India
abilities: Glycyrrhizin is about 30–50 times sweeter than sucrose
Blocks the enzyme 11β-HSD2, causing the body to hold on to salt and lose potassium
Fixes nitrogen through root-nodule bacteria
Deep runners let it survive saline, arid floodplains
edibilityNote: Root and extract flavour sweets, beer, tobacco and drinks. Regular large amounts of true liquorice can cause high blood pressure, low potassium, heart rhythm problems and, rarely, death.

uses.use: Yashtimadhu as a soothing demulcent for cough, sore throat, ulcers and as a rasayana for voice and skin
Gancao tonifies spleen qi, moistens the lungs, eases spasms and harmonises other herbs; it appears in a large share of classical formulas
Asl-us-sus for cough, chest complaints, ulcers and as a flavouring corrective in compounds
Deglycyrrhizinated liquorice (DGL) for dyspepsia; carbenoxolone, a glycyrrhetinic-acid derivative, was formerly prescribed for ulcers

medicinal.cautions: Can cause pseudohyperaldosteronism, with hypertension, oedema, low potassium and arrhythmia. Dangerous with heart or kidney disease and with diuretics, digoxin or corticosteroids. Avoid in pregnancy, as heavy intake is linked to preterm birth and effects on the child. A man in Massachusetts died in 2020 after eating a bag and a half of black liquorice daily for weeks.

fruit.description: Flat, reddish-brown pod, 1.5–3 cm, with 2–6 seeds.

seed.description: Kidney-shaped, hard-coated seeds
seed.dispersal: Gravity, water; spreads mainly by runners
seed.germination: Scarify or soak in hot water; 1–3 weeks at 20–25 °C

steps: Plant 15 cm runner sections with buds in spring, 45 cm apart
Give deep, loose soil so the roots can run
Leave undisturbed for three years
Dig in autumn, keeping runners to replant

lore: Theophrastus wrote of a sweet 'Scythian root' that let warriors go days without water. Liquorice was grown around Pontefract in Yorkshire from the medieval period, home of the Pontefract cake sweets.
funFact: Glycyrrhiza comes from the Greek for 'sweet root', and the word 'liquorice' is a corruption of it.

summary: A handsome, fiercely spiny thistle whose glossy leaves are marbled with white veins, said in legend to be drops of the Virgin Mary's milk. Its seeds yield silymarin, which is used as an antidote for death-cap mushroom poisoning.
nativeRange: Mediterranean, North Africa and South-West Asia; invasive in California, Australia and South America
abilities: Seeds contain silymarin, a flavonolignan complex that protects liver cells in lab studies
Intravenous silibinin can block uptake of death-cap toxins (amatoxins) by the liver
Grows quickly into dense, spiny thickets that grazing animals avoid
Can accumulate nitrates to levels toxic to cattle and sheep
edibilityNote: Young parts are eaten like artichoke or cardoon once the spines are removed. Plants on heavily fertilised ground can hold nitrates harmful to livestock.

uses.use: Seeds for liver and gallbladder complaints, jaundice and to increase breast milk
Seeds used for liver disorders and as a diuretic
Intravenous silibinin (Legalon SIL) used in Europe for Amanita mushroom poisoning; oral silymarin trialled for alcoholic and fatty liver disease

medicinal.cautions: Clinical trials in chronic liver disease are mixed and mostly show no clear benefit. Mild digestive upset is common, and Asteraceae allergy is possible. May lower blood sugar. Mushroom poisoning is an emergency for hospital treatment only.

fruit.description: Shiny, mottled black-brown achene with a deciduous white pappus.

seed.description: Glossy, mottled, oval seeds

grow.timeToHarvest: Seeds about 4 months after spring sowing
steps: Check whether it is a listed weed locally before planting
Sow 1 cm deep in spring, 60 cm apart
Bag flower heads with paper as they dry so the seeds are not lost
Wear thick gloves to harvest and clean the seed

lore: Dioscorides recommended thistle seeds for snakebite, and medieval Europeans dedicated the plant to the Virgin Mary, giving it the name Carduus Mariae. Culpeper wrote that it was good against 'the jaundice' and liver obstructions.
funFact: Silymarin is not one compound but a mixture of at least seven flavonolignans plus the flavonoid taxifolin. Silibinin, the main one, is the form given by drip for mushroom poisoning.

summary: A tall, sweet-smelling annual weed whose leaf glands make artemisinin, the basis of the world's front-line malaria drugs. Its rediscovery came from a 4th-century Chinese recipe and won Tu Youyou the 2015 Nobel Prize.
nativeRange: Temperate Asia, especially China; naturalised in Europe, North America and elsewhere
abilities: Glandular hairs on leaves and flowers make artemisinin, an endoperoxide that kills malaria parasites
Grows from seed to over 2 m tall in a single season
Produces enormous numbers of tiny wind-pollinated flowers
edibilityNote: Not a food. Bitter; used medicinally as tea or extract.

uses.use: Qinghao clears summer heat and 'deficiency heat' and treats intermittent fevers (malaria); Ge Hong's 4th-century recipe soaks the herb in cold water and drinks the juice
Artemisinin derivatives (artesunate, artemether, dihydroartemisinin) in artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs), the WHO-recommended treatment for malaria

medicinal.cautions: The purified drugs are strongly proven, but the WHO advises against using the dried leaf or tea to treat or prevent malaria: dosing is unreliable and it may encourage resistance. Malaria needs prompt medical treatment. Asteraceae allergy.

fruit.description: Minute, smooth, brown achenes.

seed.description: Dust-like seeds

steps: Surface-sow under cover in spring
Plant out 60–100 cm apart after frost
Harvest leaves at early bud stage, when artemisinin peaks
Dry in shade

lore: Ge Hong's Zhouhou Beiji Fang (Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies, c. 340 CE) told readers to soak a handful of qinghao in water and drink the juice for fevers. In 1971 Tu Youyou of China's secret malaria programme, Project 523, read the line and switched to a low-temperature extraction, which preserved the active compound.
funFact: Artemisinin is also made by engineered yeast. Sanofi launched semi-synthetic artemisinin production in 2013, but it struggled to compete on price with farm-grown plants.

summary: A small Andean cloud-forest tree whose bitter bark gave the world quinine, the first effective treatment for malaria. That trade shaped empires, and Britain and the Netherlands smuggled seeds out of South America to found plantations in India and Java.
nativeRange: Montane forests of the Andes in southern Ecuador and northern Peru
abilities: Bark contains quinine and quinidine, alkaloids toxic to malaria parasites and active on heart rhythm
Grows in the misty mid-elevation Andes, roughly 1,600–2,700 m
Winged seeds are carried by wind across mountain slopes
edibilityNote: Bark is not food. The small amount of quinine in tonic water is safe for most people, but bark preparations and quinine overdose are dangerous.

uses.use: Bark for fevers and chills; whether it was used before the Spanish arrived is debated by historians
'Jesuits' powder' for intermittent fevers (malaria) from the 1630s; the decisive drug against malaria for three centuries
Quinine for severe or resistant malaria (now largely replaced by artesunate); quinidine as an antiarrhythmic

medicinal.cautions: Quinine causes cinchonism: ringing ears, hearing loss, headache, nausea and blurred vision. It can trigger dangerous drops in platelets, haemolysis (especially with G6PD deficiency), low blood sugar and heart arrhythmia, and overdose can be fatal. The US FDA warns against using quinine for leg cramps.

fruit.description: Small oblong dry capsule splitting from the base.

seed.description: Flat seeds with a papery wing
seed.germination: Surface-sow on moist, shaded, acidic medium; 2–4 weeks at 20–25 °C

grow.sun: Part shade when young; sun later
steps: Sow on the surface of sterile, acidic compost in high humidity
Grow seedlings under shade cloth and mist frequently
Plant out on cool, misty, frost-free slopes
Bark was traditionally stripped in sections or the trees were coppiced

lore: Linnaeus named the genus in 1742 after the Countess of Chinchón, who legend said was cured of fever in Lima around 1638, a story historians now doubt. He also misspelled her title. A cinchona tree appears on the national coat of arms of Peru.
funFact: Quinine glows bright blue under ultraviolet light, which is why a gin and tonic fluoresces under a blacklight.

summary: A grey-leaved annual poppy whose unripe seed capsules bleed a latex that has given humanity its strongest painkillers, and some of its worst addictions. Its seeds, by contrast, are harmless enough to scatter on bread.
nativeRange: Probably derived from wild Papaver setigerum in the western Mediterranean; cultivated since the Neolithic and naturalised widely
abilities: Latex contains morphine and codeine, which act on the body's opioid receptors
Makes over 40 benzylisoquinoline alkaloids, including thebaine (precursor of many semi-synthetic opioids), papaverine and noscapine
Seed capsules release seed through a ring of pores, like a pepper pot, when shaken by wind
edibilityNote: Ripe seeds are a common food and contain almost no alkaloid. Unwashed seeds can carry morphine from the capsule, enough to cause positive drug tests, and 'poppy seed tea' has caused fatal overdoses. Latex, green capsules and straw are poisonous.

uses.use: Afyun in small amounts in sedative, anti-diarrhoeal and cough compounds; seeds (khashkhash) as a cooling nutritive
Ahiphena (introduced in the medieval period) for diarrhoea, pain and insomnia, after purification procedures
Poppy husk (yingsuqiao) to stop chronic cough and diarrhoea
Source of morphine and codeine and the raw material for semi-synthetic opioids; papaverine as a smooth-muscle relaxant

medicinal.cautions: Opioids cause dependence and addiction, and overdose depresses breathing and can kill. Cultivation and extraction are legally controlled in most countries. Never prepare home extracts from capsules or seed washings, as their strength varies wildly.

fruit.description: Smooth, rounded capsule up to 5 cm, crowned by a flat stigmatic disc, releasing seed through pores.

seed.description: Kidney-shaped, finely netted seeds, blue-black, white or brown
seed.dispersal: Shaken from capsule pores; long-lived soil seed bank
seed.germination: Sow on the surface in cool soil; 7–14 days at 10–15 °C

steps: Check national law: growing opium poppy is restricted or illegal in many places
Broadcast seed thinly in autumn or early spring
Thin to 15–20 cm, as poppies resent transplanting
For ornamental seed, cut capsules once dry and rattling

lore: Seeds and capsules have been found at the Neolithic lake village of La Marmotta near Rome (c. 5600 BCE). Between 1804 and 1817 the German pharmacist Friedrich Sertürner isolated and described morphine, which he named morphium after Morpheus, the god of dreams. Britain's opium trade triggered the Opium Wars with China (1839–42, 1856–60).
funFact: Morphine was the first alkaloid ever isolated from a plant, launching the chemistry of drugs taken from plants.

summary: A shade-loving perennial of chalky woods whose glossy, sweet black berries can kill a child. Its alkaloid atropine is an essential medicine, still used to restart slow hearts and to counter nerve agents.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western Asia (to Iran); naturalised locally elsewhere
abilities: Makes tropane alkaloids (hyoscyamine, atropine, scopolamine) that block acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors
Dilates the pupils, relaxes gut and airway muscle and speeds the heart
Some rabbits and other animals carry an enzyme, atropinesterase, that lets them eat it safely
edibilityNote: All parts are deadly, including the sweet-tasting berries, and a few berries can kill a child. Symptoms include dry mouth, flushing, dilated pupils, racing heart, delirium, hallucinations and coma.

uses.use: Leaf plasters for pain and as an antispasmodic; famously misused as a poison and in 'witches' ointments'
Atropine for slow heart rate, organophosphate and nerve-agent poisoning, before anaesthesia and to dilate pupils; scopolamine for motion sickness

medicinal.cautions: Deadly poisonous, and rubbing the eyes after handling the plant can dilate the pupils. Atropine is a prescription drug on the WHO Essential Medicines List. Never self-medicate. Treat suspected poisoning as an emergency.

fruit.description: Glossy black cherry-sized berry, 1–1.5 cm, sitting in a five-pointed green star of sepals; sweet and deadly.

seed.description: Many small, kidney-shaped, pitted brown seeds
seed.dispersal: Birds, which are less affected by the toxins
seed.germination: Slow and erratic; needs cold stratification

grow.propagation: Seed (stratified) or root division; grown only in licensed physic gardens
grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves at flowering, years 2–4 (pharmaceutical crops only)
steps: Not recommended for home gardens, especially with children or pets
In physic gardens grow behind barriers with clear labels
Wear gloves; wash hands after handling
Remove berries before they ripen in public plantings

lore: Renaissance Italian women are said to have used belladonna drops to make their pupils large and alluring. Linnaeus named the genus after Atropos, the Fate who cuts the thread of life.
funFact: Scottish chronicle tradition, retold by the 16th-century historian George Buchanan, says the Scots drugged an invading Danish army in the 11th century with drink laced with a sleep-inducing nightshade, often identified as belladonna. It is probably legend.

summary: A woody, grey-green Mediterranean sub-shrub whose very name, from the Latin salvere, means 'to be well'. Medieval doctors put it in nearly every remedy.
nativeRange: Northern and eastern Mediterranean, especially the Balkans and Adriatic coast; cultivated worldwide
abilities: Contains carnosic acid and rosmarinic acid, strong antioxidants
Leaf oil is rich in thujone, which repels insects and is toxic at high doses
Felted grey hairs shade the leaves and cut water loss in summer drought
Its hinged stamens act as a lever, dabbing pollen onto the backs of visiting bees
edibilityNote: Leaves are a culinary herb. The essential oil and very large amounts of the herb contain enough thujone to cause seizures.

uses.use: Gargles for sore throat and gum inflammation; tea to reduce sweating, for indigestion and to dry up breast milk
Maramiya tea taken after meals for stomach ache, colds and menstrual cramps
EMA-recognised for excessive sweating and mouth inflammation; small trials for menopausal hot flushes and memory

medicinal.cautions: Thujone is a convulsant, so avoid the essential oil, long-term high doses, pregnancy, breastfeeding and epilepsy. Culinary use is safe.

fruit.description: Four round dark nutlets in the calyx.

seed.description: Round, dark brown seeds

grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves lightly in year 1; fully from year 2
steps: Sow or root cuttings in spring
Plant in sun in free-draining soil
Prune lightly after flowering to stop it getting leggy
Replace plants every 4–5 years as they become woody

lore: The medieval health manual of the School of Salerno asked: 'Cur moriatur homo cui salvia crescit in horto?' ('Why should a man die who grows sage in his garden?'). Charlemagne's Capitulare de villis (c. 800) ordered it grown on imperial estates.
funFact: Salvia is the largest genus in the mint family, with roughly 1,000 species, and since 2017 it has included rosemary.

otherNames: Iklīl al-jabal إكليل الجبل (Arabic, 'crown of the mountain')
summary: An aromatic evergreen shrub of sea cliffs and garrigue, the herb of remembrance at weddings and funerals. Botanists moved it out of Rosmarinus and into the sage genus in 2017 after DNA studies.
nativeRange: Mediterranean basin, from Portugal and Morocco to Turkey
abilities: Carnosic acid and carnosol make it one of the most effective natural food antioxidants
Needle-like, rolled leaves with hairy undersides survive drought and salt spray
Flowers in late winter and early spring, an important early source of nectar for bees
edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers are a culinary herb. The undiluted essential oil is toxic if swallowed and can trigger seizures.

uses.use: Tea and wine infusions for memory, headache, poor circulation and indigestion; spirits rubbed on aching joints and the scalp
Iklil-ul-jabal used as a nervine and brain tonic, carminative and for rheumatic pain
Azir leaf infusions for digestive complaints, diabetes and as a general tonic
EMA traditional-use monograph for dyspepsia and as a bath additive for muscle and joint pain

medicinal.cautions: Only a few small clinical trials exist, so the evidence is weak. The essential oil can provoke seizures in high doses, so avoid it with epilepsy and in pregnancy. Medicinal doses may interact with anticoagulants and diuretics.

fruit.description: Four small brown nutlets.

seed.description: Small, oval, light-brown seeds
seed.germination: Low and slow; 2–4 weeks at 18–22 °C. Cuttings are far easier

steps: Root 10 cm cuttings in gritty compost in late summer
Plant in the hottest, best-drained spot available
Water only in prolonged drought
Trim after flowering, never into bare wood

lore: In Hamlet, Ophelia says 'There's rosemary, that's for remembrance'. In medieval and Tudor England sprigs were carried at both weddings and funerals. 'Hungary water', a rosemary-based spirit, was one of Europe's first alcohol-based perfumes.
funFact: Rosemary extract is approved in the EU as a food antioxidant under the code E 392.

otherNames: Ṣaʿtar / Zaʿtar (Arabic, used loosely for thyme-like herbs)
summary: A tiny-leaved, low woody shrub of sun-baked Mediterranean hills whose oil, thymol, was among the first antiseptics of modern medicine. Wild populations come in distinct 'chemotypes' that smell quite different.
nativeRange: Western Mediterranean: Spain, southern France, Italy
abilities: Thymol and carvacrol in its oil kill many bacteria and fungi
Forms distinct chemotypes (thymol, carvacrol, linalool, geraniol and others) that sort out by local soil and frost
Survives summer drought by shedding some leaves and thriving in shallow, stony soil
Small flowers are heavily worked by honeybees; thyme honey is a prized Mediterranean speciality
edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers are a classic culinary herb. The essential oil is irritating and toxic in quantity.

uses.use: Tea and syrup for coughs, whooping cough and bronchitis; antiseptic washes for wounds
Satar (various thyme species) for coughs, digestive complaints and intestinal worms
Thyme extract, often combined with ivy or primrose, approved in Germany for coughs from bronchitis; thymol in mouthwashes

medicinal.cautions: Trials of thyme combination products for acute bronchitis are positive. The essential oil irritates skin and mucous membranes and should not be swallowed. People allergic to other Lamiaceae may react. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Four minute, dark nutlets in the calyx.

seed.description: Tiny, round, dark brown

grow.soil: Poor, stony, alkaline, very well drained
steps: Surface-sow under cover in spring, or root tip cuttings
Plant in full sun in gritty soil
Shear after flowering to keep plants compact
Renew every 3–4 years

lore: Thymol was first isolated by the German apothecary Caspar Neumann in 1719. When the First World War cut off German supplies, thymol ran short just as it was urgently needed for dressing soldiers' wounds, and new production started in Britain and India.
funFact: Thymol is used by beekeepers to treat honeybee colonies against the parasitic varroa mite.

otherNames: Nagadamani (Sanskrit, as applied in some Ayurvedic texts)
summary: A tall, silver-backed roadside perennial named for Artemis, goddess of women and childbirth. It is the first of the Anglo-Saxon Nine Herbs, and in late summer one of Europe's worst hay-fever plants.
nativeRange: Temperate Europe, Asia and North Africa; invasive in eastern North America
abilities: Silvery, felted leaf undersides reflect heat and carry aromatic oil glands
Spreads by rhizomes and can regrow from small root fragments, making it hard to eradicate
Releases huge amounts of wind-borne pollen; the allergen Art v 1 is a leading cause of late-summer hay fever
Its aromatic compounds repel insects; sprigs were laid in shoes and linen
edibilityNote: Used as a bitter flavouring for fatty meats and goose and, historically, in gruit ale before hops. It contains thujone, so avoid large amounts and avoid it entirely in pregnancy. Can cross-react in people with celery or spice allergies.

uses.use: Bitter tea for poor appetite, indigestion and irregular or painful menstruation; laid in shoes against travel-weariness
Mugwort leaf (ai ye, mainly the related A. argyi) is dried into moxa and burned over acupuncture points (moxibustion)
Leaves used for worms, fevers and menstrual complaints

medicinal.cautions: Avoid in pregnancy, as it was traditionally used to provoke menstruation and abortion. Thujone toxicity is possible at high doses. Pollen and food allergy (the 'mugwort–celery–spice syndrome'). Asteraceae allergy.

fruit.description: Minute brown achenes without a pappus.

seed.description: Tiny, oblong, brown seeds

grow.soil: Any; thrives on disturbed, nitrogen-rich ground
grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves from year 1, just before flowering
steps: Grow in a sunk container or a contained bed, as it is invasive in North America
Surface-sow or plant divisions in spring
Cut leafy tops just as the flower buds form
Hang to dry and strip the leaves

lore: The Old English Nine Herbs Charm in the 10th-century Lacnunga manuscript names Mucgwyrt first, calling it 'the oldest of plants'. Pliny wrote that a traveller carrying artemisia would not feel weary.
funFact: On St John's Eve, medieval Europeans wore mugwort garlands ('St John's girdle') and threw them into the midsummer bonfire to burn away bad luck.

otherNames: Yì zhū qiánmá 异株荨麻 (Chinese)
summary: A plant armed with thousands of tiny glass-tipped syringes that inject an irritant cocktail into the skin. It is also nutritious, a source of fine linen-like fibre, and food for some of Europe's most familiar butterflies.
nativeRange: Europe, temperate Asia and western North Africa; with native subspecies in North America
abilities: Stinging hairs have silica tips that snap off and inject histamine, acetylcholine, serotonin and oxalic and tartaric acids
Grows thickly wherever soil is rich in phosphate and nitrogen, marking old settlements for centuries
Stem fibres are long and strong enough to spin and weave into cloth
Caterpillar food for peacock, small tortoiseshell, red admiral and comma butterflies
edibleParts: young leaves and tops (cooked or dried)
edibilityNote: Young tops are cooked as soup, pesto or tea; heat or drying destroys the sting. Use gloves when picking. Eat young growth before flowering; older leaves become gritty with cystoliths.

uses.use: Nettle tea as a spring tonic and diuretic; 'urtication', beating aching joints with fresh nettles, for rheumatism
Anjura seeds and leaves for cough, kidney stones and as a diuretic
Native nettles were used by many nations, including Pacific Northwest peoples, for fibre, as food, and by urtication for arthritis
Root extracts for urinary symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia; leaf for arthritis and allergic rhinitis

medicinal.cautions: Diuretic effects may interact with lithium, blood-pressure and diabetes drugs. Mild digestive upset. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy. The sting can cause severe reactions in rare cases.

fruit.description: Minute flattened achenes on drooping female catkins (plants are mostly single-sexed).

seed.description: Tiny oval greenish-brown seeds
seed.dispersal: Wind, water and animals; long-lived seed bank

grow.soil: Rich, moist, high in nitrogen and phosphate
steps: Plant a rhizome piece in a corner or a sunk container
Cut back hard several times a year to keep a supply of young tops
Harvest with gloves before flowering
Leave a patch uncut over summer for butterfly caterpillars

lore: In Hans Christian Andersen's The Wild Swans (1838), the heroine weaves nettle shirts to break a spell on her brothers. During the First World War, Germany made uniform cloth from nettle fibre when cotton was blockaded.
funFact: A Bronze Age burial cloth from Lusehøj in Denmark, about 2,800 years old, turned out to be nettle fibre, and its chemistry suggests the nettles grew in Austria.

summary: The world's most familiar weed. Each flower head is a cluster of up to 200 florets, and most of its seeds are clones made without pollination. Every part is edible and its bitter roots and leaves have long been used as a liver and kidney remedy.
nativeRange: Eurasia; now naturalised on every continent except Antarctica
abilities: Sets seed asexually (apomixis): most seeds are genetic copies of the parent
Its pappus parachute creates a stable 'separated vortex ring' of air, a kind of flight unknown before 2018
Deep taproot regrows from fragments and draws up minerals
Flowers from early spring, an important early nectar and pollen source
edibilityNote: All parts are edible; young leaves are less bitter. Avoid plants from sprayed lawns or roadsides. People allergic to Asteraceae or latex may react.

uses.use: Leaf as a diuretic ('pissenlit'); root as a bitter tonic for liver, gallbladder and digestion
Pugongying clears heat and toxins, for breast abscess, boils, sore throat and urinary infections
Adopted after European introduction by several nations, such as the Ojibwe and Iroquois, as a spring green and for heartburn and kidney complaints

medicinal.cautions: Only one small pilot trial supports the diuretic effect. Can interact with lithium, diuretics and some antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin. Avoid with gallbladder obstruction. Asteraceae and latex allergy.

fruit.description: Ribbed achenes on a slender beak topped with a parachute, forming the 'clock'.

seed.description: Olive-brown spiny achene with white pappus

grow.soil: Any; deeper soil gives larger roots
grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves 6–8 weeks; roots in autumn of year 1–2
steps: Scatter seed on the surface in spring
Blanch leaves under a pot for a week for milder salad greens
Pick flowers for wine or fritters at midday when fully open
Dig roots in autumn, roast and grind for 'coffee'

lore: The genus name came into medieval Latin from the Arabic and Persian tarakhshaqūq, a plant discussed by Arabic physicians around the 10th–11th centuries. The English name comes from the French dent de lion, 'lion's tooth', after the jagged leaves.
funFact: In 2018 Edinburgh researchers showed that a dandelion seed's bristly parachute is about 90% empty space, yet it traps a stable bubble of swirling air that keeps it aloft.

otherNames: White man's footprint (English, from Indigenous American usage)
summary: A flat-rosetted weed of paths and farmyards so tough it thrives where it is trodden on daily. European colonists spread it around the world on their boots, and it has been one of folk medicine's standard wound leaves for at least a thousand years.
nativeRange: Europe and northern & central Asia; now cosmopolitan
abilities: Flat rosette and tough, ribbed leaves survive heavy trampling
Seeds turn sticky with mucilage when wet and hitch rides on feet, hooves and tyres
Leaves contain aucubin and acteoside, studied for anti-inflammatory and wound-healing effects
A single plant can produce many thousands of long-lived seeds
edibilityNote: Young leaves can be eaten raw or cooked, but older leaves are stringy. Avoid plants from sprayed or polluted ground.

uses.use: Chewed or crushed leaf on stings, bites, cuts and burns; tea for coughs and diarrhoea
Adopted by many nations after European contact as a poultice for wounds, snakebite and boils
Bartang seeds and leaves as a cooling demulcent for dysentery and coughs
Plantago herb and seed (cheqiancao, cheqianzi) to drain damp, for urinary difficulty and diarrhoea

medicinal.cautions: Generally safe. The pollen is allergenic. In 1997 supplements labelled 'plantain' were found to be contaminated with Digitalis, so buy only from reputable sources.

fruit.description: Small capsule whose top pops off like a lid, on dense spikes.

seed.description: Small, angular brown seeds that become sticky when wet
seed.dispersal: Sticky seeds carried on feet, animals and vehicles

steps: Scatter seed on the surface in spring
Leave in a lawn or path edge where it is wanted
Pick young leaves for food or poultices
Remove seed spikes if you want to stop it spreading

lore: The Old English Nine Herbs Charm calls it Wegbrade, 'way-broad', the 'mother of herbs' that withstands carts and riders. Longfellow's Song of Hiawatha (1855) records the Indigenous name 'White-Man's Foot'.
funFact: The name Plantago comes from the Latin planta, 'sole of the foot', after its flat leaves lying on the ground like footprints.

summary: A biennial that spends its first year as a rosette of leaves as soft as felt, then sends up a 2 m spike of sulphur-yellow flowers. Its dried stalks, dipped in tallow, were once burned as torches.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Asia; naturalised and invasive in North America, Australia and elsewhere
abilities: Dense branched hairs shield the leaves from sun, drought and grazing
Seeds stay viable in soil for many decades
Colonises bare, burned or disturbed ground quickly
A single plant can bear over 100,000 seeds
edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers are used for tea only, and the irritating hairs must be strained out through fine cloth. Seeds contain saponins and have been used as fish poison; do not eat them.

uses.use: Flower and leaf tea for coughs, bronchitis and sore throat; flower oil dropped into the ear for earache
Adopted after introduction by nations including the Navajo, Cherokee and Iroquois, who smoked or brewed the leaves for coughs and asthma

medicinal.cautions: Strain teas carefully, as the hairs irritate the throat. Do not put oil in the ear if the eardrum may be perforated. The seeds are toxic.

fruit.description: Woolly, egg-shaped two-valved capsule with many seeds.

seed.description: Tiny, pitted, brown seeds
seed.dispersal: Shaken out by wind and passing animals; long-lived seed bank

steps: Check local status first, as it is invasive in some regions
Surface-sow in spring or autumn
Harvest leaves from first-year rosettes and flowers daily in year 2
Cut spikes before seed sets to prevent spread

lore: Dried mullein stalks dipped in tallow were burned as torches ('hag's tapers'), and the woolly leaves were used as lamp wicks and as linings for shoes. Dioscorides recommended phlomos for coughs and eye complaints.
funFact: In W. J. Beal's buried-seed experiment, begun in Michigan in 1879, seeds of the related moth mullein still germinated after 120 years.

summary: A velvety, pale-pink mallow of salt marshes whose roots are so full of slime that they soothe sore throats. The original marshmallow sweet was made from them.
