nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western & Central Asia; especially coastal salt marshes and damp ground
abilities: Roots are rich in mucilage, which coats and soothes mucous membranes
Tolerates brackish, salt-influenced soils
Velvety hairs cover the whole plant
edibilityNote: All parts are edible; roots were boiled and fried, and leaves eaten as a pot herb. Wild populations are scarce in some countries, so use cultivated plants.

uses.use: Cold root infusion and syrup for dry cough, sore throat and gastritis; poultices for inflamed skin
Khatmi root and seed as a demulcent for cough, urinary burning and in softening poultices
EMA traditional-use monograph for dry cough and mouth/throat irritation

medicinal.cautions: The mucilage may slow the absorption of other medicines, so take them an hour apart. May lower blood sugar.

fruit.description: Flat ring of nutlets like a small round cheese.

seed.description: Kidney-shaped, brown seeds
seed.germination: Benefits from cold stratification; 2–3 weeks at 15–20 °C

grow.soil: Moist, rich; tolerates heavy and slightly saline soil
steps: Sow in spring after chilling the seed in the fridge for 3–4 weeks
Plant 60 cm apart in moist soil
Harvest leaves before flowering
Dig roots in autumn of year 2, peel and dry

lore: Theophrastus and Dioscorides recommended althaia, from the Greek althein, 'to heal'. In 19th-century France, confectioners whipped the root mucilage with sugar and egg white into pâte de guimauve; gelatine later replaced the root.
funFact: Today's marshmallows contain no marshmallow: gelatine replaced the root in the late 19th century.

summary: A pepper-family shrub from Vanuatu whose root drink brings calm and sociability without clouding the mind like alcohol. It is the ceremonial drink of the Pacific, and every plant is a sterile clone carried from island to island by voyagers.
nativeRange: Domesticated in northern Vanuatu from wild Piper wichmannii; spread by people across Melanesia, Polynesia and Micronesia
abilities: Roots contain kavalactones, which act on GABA-A receptors and sodium channels, relaxing muscles and easing anxiety
Cultivated kava is sterile and propagated entirely from stem cuttings by people
Kava chemistry differs between cultivars, which Pacific growers classify by effect
edibleParts: root and rhizome (as a cold-water drink)
edibilityNote: Traditionally drunk as a water extract of fresh or dried root. Use only peeled root and rhizome of 'noble' cultivars; leaves, stems and 'tudei' (two-day) cultivars are linked to more side effects. Do not combine with alcohol or drive.

uses.use: Drunk ceremonially and socially; also for urinary complaints, headaches, insomnia and to calm nerves
In Vanuatu and Fiji, for relaxation, sleep and pain, and in ritual to honour guests and chiefs
Standardised extracts trialled for generalised anxiety disorder, with mixed but partly positive results

medicinal.cautions: Reports of severe liver injury led to bans in several European countries from 2002; Germany's ban was overturned in court in 2014. Risk seems linked to extract type and plant parts. Heavy use causes a scaly skin rash (kava dermopathy). Avoid with liver disease, alcohol, sedatives, Parkinson's disease, pregnancy and breastfeeding.

seed.description: Cultivated kava does not set viable seed

grow.soil: Loose, rich, well-drained volcanic or forest loam
steps: Lay node-bearing stem sections on moist soil, half-buried, under light shade
Keep warm (above 20 °C) and humid; it cannot tolerate frost or drought
Mulch and weed for several years
Dig the whole root mass at 3–5 years, keeping stems to replant

lore: At the Tongan royal kava ceremony (taumafa kava), seating and the order of serving show each chief's rank, and it is an essential part of a king's coronation. Captain Cook's naturalists, including Georg Forster, described the drink in 1777.
funFact: Because cultivated kava cannot set seed, every kava plant across the Pacific descends from cuttings carried by people, some over thousands of kilometres of open ocean.

summary: A fast-growing, drought-hardy tree from the Himalayan foothills whose leaves, pods and flowers feed millions across the tropics. Its crushed seeds can clear muddy water.
nativeRange: Sub-Himalayan foothills of north-western India, Pakistan and Nepal; planted throughout the tropics
abilities: Can grow several metres in its first year from seed or cuttings
Seed proteins carry a positive charge that clumps suspended particles and bacteria, clarifying water
Leaves are rich in protein, vitamin A precursors, calcium and iron
Survives long dry seasons by shedding leaves and storing water in a swollen root
edibilityNote: Leaves, pods and flowers are widely eaten cooked. Root and root bark contain toxic alkaloids such as spirochin, and the root's horseradish taste has led to poisonings. Avoid root and bark, especially in pregnancy.

uses.use: Shigru bark, leaves and seeds for swellings, joint pain, worms, abscesses and as a pungent digestive
Sahajna and ben-seed oil applied for rheumatism and gout, and taken for liver and spleen enlargement
Zogale leaves used for malnutrition, fevers, diabetes and to increase breast milk
Malunggay leaves eaten in soup by nursing mothers in the Philippines to boost milk supply

medicinal.cautions: Most evidence comes from animal and small human studies. Root and bark are toxic and can cause miscarriage. May lower blood sugar and blood pressure, and may interact with thyroid, diabetes and blood-pressure drugs.

fruit.description: Long, ribbed, three-sided pod, 20–50 cm, eaten green as a vegetable ('drumstick').

seed.description: Round, dark-brown oily seeds with three papery wings
seed.germination: Fast; 5–12 days at 25–35 °C; no pre-treatment needed

grow.soil: Sandy or loamy, well-drained; hates waterlogging
grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves from 2–3 months; pods from 6–12 months
steps: Sow seeds 2 cm deep in warm, well-drained soil
Plant out in full sun, protected from frost
Cut back the leader at 1–1.5 m to encourage a bushy, easy-to-pick tree
Harvest leaves continuously and pods while they snap cleanly

lore: The Sushruta and Charaka Samhitas list shigru among useful pungent herbs. Ben oil, pressed from the seeds, was traded to Europe where watchmakers prized it for lubricating fine mechanisms because it does not go rancid quickly.
funFact: In some trials a few crushed moringa seeds per litre cut the cloudiness of river water by over 90%.

summary: A small, creeping, succulent-leaved marsh herb found in wetlands across the tropics. Ayurveda prizes it as a medhya rasayana, a tonic for memory and learning, and it is one of the better-studied herbal 'nootropics'.
nativeRange: Pantropical and warm-temperate wetlands of Asia, Africa, Australia and the Americas (including the southern USA)
abilities: Contains bacosides, saponins studied for effects on memory and the survival of nerve cells
Grows submerged or emerged, rooting at every node
Tolerates brackish water
Takes up heavy metals from polluted water, which makes clean sourcing important
edibilityNote: Eaten as a bitter herb in parts of South and Southeast Asia. Collect only from clean water, as it accumulates heavy metals.

uses.use: Medhya rasayana for memory, learning, anxiety and epilepsy; given as juice, ghee (brahmi ghrita) or powder
Nirbrahmi for fever, nervous disorders and as a brain tonic
Standardised extracts trialled for memory in healthy adults and the elderly, with small benefits in some trials

compounds: bacoside A (bacoside A3, bacopaside II, bacopasaponin C)
medicinal.cautions: Effects on memory are modest and take 8–12 weeks to appear. Common side effects are nausea, cramps and diarrhoea. May slow the heart and interact with thyroid drugs and sedatives. Choose products tested for heavy metals. Avoid in pregnancy.

fruit.season: Most of the year in the tropics
fruit.description: Small ovoid capsule with many tiny seeds.

seed.description: Minute seeds
seed.germination: Rarely grown from seed; cuttings root within days

grow.water: Very high: bog, pond edge or submerged
steps: Push stem cuttings into wet mud or a pot standing in water
Keep warm (above 15 °C) and constantly wet
Snip shoot tips regularly to keep it bushy
Use clean water only

lore: The Charaka Samhita lists brahmi among the medhya (intellect-promoting) rasayanas. Scholars still debate whether some classical references to 'brahmi' meant this plant or Centella asiatica.
funFact: Bacopa is a common aquarium plant, and the very same species is sold in health shops as a memory tonic.

otherNames: Bai bua bok ใบบัวบก (Thai)
summary: A creeping herb of damp tropical ground with kidney-shaped leaves, eaten as salad and juice from Sri Lanka to Vietnam. Its triterpenes are used in wound-healing and scar creams.
nativeRange: Tropical and subtropical Asia, Africa (including Madagascar), Australia and the western Pacific
abilities: Asiaticoside and madecassoside stimulate collagen synthesis in wound and scar models
Spreads quickly by runners, rooting at each node to form a ground carpet
Thrives in waterlogged and semi-shaded ground
edibilityNote: Eaten raw in Sri Lankan gotu kola sambol, as Thai bai bua bok juice and as Vietnamese rau má drink. Wash well and avoid plants from polluted water.

uses.use: Mandukaparni as a medhya rasayana for memory and as a remedy for skin disease and wounds
Jixuecao clears heat and damp, for jaundice, heatstroke, bruising and swellings
Used in Madagascar and elsewhere for leprosy sores, wounds and skin complaints
Titrated extract for chronic venous insufficiency; topical creams (e.g. Madécassol) for wounds and scars

medicinal.cautions: Rare liver injury has been reported with oral products. May cause drowsiness and add to sedatives. Topical use can cause contact dermatitis. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Small, flattened, ribbed fruit splitting into two mericarps.

seed.description: Small flattened mericarps
seed.dispersal: Water and soil; mostly spreads by runners
seed.germination: Slow and erratic; runners are easier

steps: Plant rooted runner sections in moist, rich soil
Keep constantly damp and lightly shaded
Harvest outer leaves with stalks regularly
Grow in a container or contained bed to stop it spreading

lore: Jixuecao is listed in the Shennong Bencao Jing, and mandukaparni in the Charaka Samhita. The French pharmaceutical name Madécassol comes from 'Madécasse', the old French word for Madagascar, an early supply source.
funFact: Despite looking like a tiny lily pad, gotu kola belongs to the carrot family, Apiaceae.

summary: An autumn-flowering crocus whose three crimson stigmas, picked by hand, are the world's most expensive spice. It is a sterile triploid that has not set seed in thousands of years and survives only because people replant its corms.
nativeRange: Known only in cultivation; arose from the wild Crocus cartwrightianus in Bronze Age Greece. Grown mainly in Iran, Kashmir, Spain, Greece and Morocco
abilities: Stigmas contain crocin, a water-soluble carotenoid that dyes intensely golden
Safranal, formed from picrocrocin as the stigmas dry, gives saffron its hay-like aroma
Sterile triploid: every plant is a clone, multiplied only by daughter corms
Flowers in autumn, before its leaves fully emerge
edibilityNote: Safe in culinary amounts (a few threads). Doses of about 5 g or more are toxic, and around 12–20 g has been reported as potentially lethal. Do not confuse it with the deadly autumn crocus (Colchicum autumnale), which looks similar but has six stamens and no long red stigmas.

uses.use: Zafran as an exhilarant (mufarrih) for melancholy, a heart tonic and an aphrodisiac
Kunkuma for skin complexion, menstrual complaints, cough and as a rejuvenating tonic in milk
Zanghonghua ('Tibetan red flower', also fanhonghua) to invigorate blood, cool the blood and calm the spirit, for amenorrhoea, postpartum pain and low mood
Small trials of 30 mg/day extract for mild to moderate depression, with positive results

medicinal.cautions: Depression trials are small and mostly from one region. High doses stimulate the uterus, so avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy. Large doses are toxic. Saffron is widely adulterated with safflower, turmeric or dyed fibres.

seed.description: Sterile; does not produce viable seed

steps: Plant corms 10 cm deep and 10 cm apart in late summer
Water lightly in autumn if dry
Pick flowers in the morning as they open and pluck out the three red stigmas
Dry stigmas gently and store airtight in the dark; lift and divide crowded corms every 3–4 years

lore: The 'Saffron Gatherers' frescoes at Akrotiri on Thera (c. 1600 BCE) show women gathering crocus stigmas and a monkey presenting saffron to a goddess. Iran today grows the great majority of the world's saffron.
funFact: About 150,000 flowers are needed for one kilogram of dried saffron.

summary: A tall rainforest herb of the ginger family whose small green pods hold the 'queen of spices'. It flavours Arabic coffee, chai and Scandinavian buns, and is the third most expensive spice by weight after saffron and vanilla.
nativeRange: Moist evergreen forests of the Western Ghats in southern India (and Sri Lanka)
abilities: Seeds hold an essential oil rich in 1,8-cineole and α-terpinyl acetate
Flowering stems creep along the ground, so pods form at the base of the plant
Grows in the deep shade of the forest understorey
edibilityNote: Safe as a spice.

uses.use: Ela for indigestion, nausea, bad breath, cough and to balance the heaviness of other foods and medicines
Qaqula / heel khurd as a carminative, heart and stomach tonic, and to stop vomiting
Cardamom-spiced coffee and chewed seeds for digestion and freshening breath

medicinal.cautions: Safe in food amounts. Medicinal amounts are traditionally avoided with gallstones, as they may trigger colic.

fruit.description: Pale green, three-sided oval pod, 1–2 cm, holding 15–20 sticky black seeds.

seed.description: Angular, wrinkled, dark-brown seeds
seed.germination: Fresh seed; 3–6 weeks at 25 °C in shade

steps: Plant divisions under 50–70% shade in rich soil
Keep moist and humid all year
Pick pods just before full ripeness, every few weeks
Dry pods slowly to keep their green colour

lore: Cardamom-scented qahwa is a symbol of hospitality across the Arabian Peninsula. Guatemala became the world's largest exporter after a German coffee planter introduced the plant there around 1914.
funFact: Most of the world's green cardamom now comes not from India but from Guatemala, where hardly any is eaten locally.

otherNames: Al-ḥabba al-sawdāʾ / Ḥabbat al-baraka (Arabic, 'black seed' / 'blessed seed')
summary: A delicate, pale-blue-flowered annual of the buttercup family whose small, pungent black seeds are sprinkled on naan and pastries. A hadith calls them a cure for every disease except death.
nativeRange: Probably South-West Asia and the eastern Mediterranean; ancient crop, wild origin uncertain
abilities: Seeds contain thymoquinone, studied for anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and blood-sugar-lowering effects
Inflated capsule of fused follicles protects the seeds
Completes its life cycle in about four months
edibilityNote: Seeds are a common spice in South Asian, Middle Eastern and Turkish breads and pickles. The oil applied to skin can cause contact dermatitis.

uses.use: Black seed and its oil taken daily as a general tonic, based on the hadith of its blessing
Shoneez / kalonji for asthma, cough, flatulence, worms, skin disease and as a diuretic
Upakunchika for digestion, fever, menstrual and lactation complaints
Small trials of seed or oil for blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar and asthma

medicinal.cautions: Trials are mostly small and short. May lower blood sugar and blood pressure and add to the effect of related drugs. Possible bleeding risk with anticoagulants. Large doses are traditionally avoided in pregnancy. Cases of kidney injury and contact dermatitis have been reported.

fruit.description: Inflated capsule of 3–7 fused follicles, each with many seeds.

seed.description: Matte black, angular, trigonous seeds
seed.germination: 7–14 days at 15–20 °C; sow 1 cm deep (darkness aids germination)

steps: Sow directly in spring (or autumn in mild climates), as it dislikes transplanting
Thin to 15–20 cm
Cut stems when the capsules turn brown and dry
Dry in paper bags and shake out the seeds

lore: Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet Muhammad saying that black seed is a cure for every disease except death. Dioscorides called it melanthion and recommended it for headache and catarrh.
funFact: Despite the name 'black cumin', Nigella is no relation of cumin: it belongs to the buttercup family, and its garden cousin is love-in-a-mist.

summary: A clover-like legume whose bitter-sweet seeds smell of maple syrup and whose leaves are a staple green in Indian cooking. Its name means 'Greek hay', because Romans grew it as fodder.
nativeRange: Eastern Mediterranean and Western Asia; ancient crop, now grown widely (India is the largest producer)
abilities: Seeds contain sotolon, a compound so potent its maple aroma passes into sweat and urine
Seed gum (galactomannan) swells in water and slows sugar absorption
Fixes nitrogen through root-nodule bacteria
Seeds contain diosgenin, once a raw material for synthesising steroid hormones
edibilityNote: Widely eaten. People allergic to peanuts or chickpeas may react to it.

uses.use: Methika for poor appetite, diabetes (prameha), joint pain and to increase breast milk
Hulba as a demulcent for cough and chest, and in poultices to ripen boils
Hulba drink after childbirth and for stomach complaints; Yemeni hilbeh paste as a digestive
Huluba to warm the kidneys and dispel cold, for hernia pain and cold in the legs

medicinal.cautions: Small trials show modest falls in blood sugar. May cause low blood sugar with diabetes drugs, and may interact with warfarin. Stimulates the uterus, so avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy. Causes a maple odour in sweat and urine, and in breastfed babies this has been mistaken for maple syrup urine disease. Can cause bloating.

fruit.description: Slender, beaked pod 10–15 cm long with 10–20 seeds.

seed.description: Hard, rhomboid, yellow-brown seeds with a deep diagonal groove

grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves in 3–4 weeks; seed in 3–4 months
steps: Sow seed 1 cm deep in cool weather
Cut leaves for greens when 10–15 cm tall
For seed, let pods dry yellow on the plant
Thresh and store seeds dry

lore: Columella and Cato wrote of fenugreek as cattle fodder. Charlemagne's Capitulare de villis (c. 800) included it among plants to grow on his estates.
funFact: A mysterious maple-syrup smell that drifted over Manhattan several times from 2005 was traced in 2009 to a New Jersey factory processing fenugreek seed.

summary: A small yellow-flowered desert shrub whose leaves and pods are among the world's most used laxatives. It was introduced to medicine by medieval Arab physicians and still sold in pharmacies everywhere.
nativeRange: North-east Africa (Egypt, Sudan, Somalia), the Arabian Peninsula and across to Pakistan and India
abilities: Contains sennosides, inactive 'prodrugs' that gut bacteria convert into rhein anthrone in the colon
Survives extreme heat and drought in desert wadis
Flat pods carry the seeds on the wind
edibilityNote: Not a food. Leaves and pods are used only as a laxative medicine.

uses.use: Sana makki as a purgative of black bile and phlegm, in compounds for skin disease, joint pain and melancholy
Leaves as a purgative (virechana) and for constipation
Fanxieye (introduced from abroad) to purge heat accumulation and relieve constipation
Standardised sennoside tablets as an over-the-counter stimulant laxative and for bowel preparation

medicinal.cautions: For short-term use only (about 1–2 weeks). Causes cramps and diarrhoea. Prolonged use or abuse causes potassium loss, dependence and melanosis coli, and low potassium can be dangerous with digoxin or diuretics. Do not use with bowel obstruction, inflammatory bowel disease, unexplained abdominal pain or in young children.

fruit.description: Flat, papery, oblong pod 4–6 cm, greenish-brown, with 5–7 seeds.

seed.description: Flat, heart-shaped, greyish-green seeds

steps: Soak seed overnight and sow in warm, sandy soil
Thin to 30–45 cm and water sparingly
Strip leaflets before flowering and pick pods as they mature
Dry in shade to keep the colour

lore: Medieval Arab physicians brought senna into medicine; the word comes from Arabic sanā. 'Alexandrian senna' was named after the Egyptian port it was shipped from, and 'Tinnevelly senna' after the district in Tamil Nadu where it was later grown.
funFact: Senna leaf does nothing until it reaches the colon, where gut bacteria break the sennosides into the active laxative compound.

otherNames: Luǎn yè chēqián 卵叶车前 (Chinese)
summary: A small, woolly desert plantain whose seed husks swell to many times their volume in water, forming a soft gel. The husk is the world's most widely used bulk-forming fibre supplement and laxative.
nativeRange: Canary Islands and the Mediterranean, North Africa and West Asia to Pakistan and north-western India; cultivated mainly in Gujarat and Rajasthan
abilities: Seed husk mucilage (an arabinoxylan) absorbs many times its weight in water
Gel softens stool, slows sugar absorption and binds bile acids, lowering LDL cholesterol
Completes its life cycle in about four months of the cool dry season
edibilityNote: Husk is taken stirred into plenty of water or used in gluten-free baking. Always take it with enough fluid.

uses.use: Isapghol as a cooling demulcent for dysentery, diarrhoea, constipation and urinary burning
Husk for constipation, diarrhoea and to soothe the gut (introduced via Persian medicine)
Bulk-forming laxative; for irritable bowel syndrome and as a cholesterol-lowering fibre (FDA heart-health claim, 1998)

medicinal.cautions: Take with at least a full glass of water: dry husk can swell and choke or block the oesophagus or bowel. Do not use with bowel obstruction or difficulty swallowing. Take other medicines 1–2 hours apart. Inhaled dust has caused asthma and anaphylaxis in healthcare and factory workers.

fruit.description: Small capsule on dense spikes with two boat-shaped seeds.

seed.description: Boat-shaped, pinkish-grey seeds coated in a translucent husk
seed.dispersal: Seeds turn sticky when wet and cling to animals

grow.zones: Annual; cool-season crop in warm climates (USDA 8–11)
grow.water: Low; dry weather at ripening is essential
steps: Sow broadcast in the cool season on fine, well-drained soil
Irrigate lightly and only as needed
Harvest when spikes turn reddish-brown, in dry weather (rain at ripening makes seeds swell and shatter)
Thresh and mill to separate the husk

lore: Persian physicians named it asp-ghol, 'horse's ear', after the shape of the seed. It entered Indian practice through Unani medicine under the Mughals, and India now grows most of the world's supply.
funFact: Stirred into water, psyllium husk sets into a thick gel within minutes, which is why bakers use it as a binder in gluten-free bread.

summary: A leafless, broom-like gymnosperm of the steppes whose green jointed stems contain ephedrine. For two thousand years it has been a Chinese remedy for colds and asthma; in the 20th century it became a decongestant drug, and later a deadly diet supplement.
nativeRange: Northern China, Mongolia and adjacent Russia
abilities: Makes ephedrine and pseudoephedrine, which mimic adrenaline, open the airways and raise heart rate and blood pressure
Leaves are reduced to tiny scales; the green stems do the photosynthesis
A gymnosperm related to conifers, with fleshy red seed cones instead of flowers and fruit
Spreading roots bind sandy steppe soils
edibilityNote: Not a food. The stems are potent stimulants.

uses.use: Mahuang to release the exterior and induce sweating in wind-cold colds, calm wheezing and promote urination; core herb of Mahuang Tang
Ephedra in formulas such as kakkonto for early colds and stiffness
Ephedrine for low blood pressure during anaesthesia; pseudoephedrine as a nasal decongestant

medicinal.cautions: Can cause high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, seizures and sudden death. The US FDA banned ephedra dietary supplements in 2004 after many adverse events and deaths. Dangerous with heart disease, thyroid disease, MAOIs and other stimulants. Pseudoephedrine sales are restricted because it is a methamphetamine precursor.

fruit.type: Fleshy seed cone (not a true fruit)
fruit.description: Red, berry-like cone of fleshy bracts around 1–2 seeds.

seed.description: Dark brown, ovoid seeds
seed.dispersal: Birds and small mammals eat the fleshy cones

steps: Grow only where legal; possession is restricted in some countries
Sow in a gritty, sandy mix in spring
Plant in full sun in a dry bed
Water rarely; it rots in wet soil

lore: The Shennong Bencao Jing lists mahuang for coughs and fevers, and Zhang Zhongjing's Shanghan Lun (c. 200 CE) built a whole family of formulas around it. In 1885 the Japanese chemist Nagai Nagayoshi isolated ephedrine, and in the 1920s Chen and Schmidt introduced it to Western medicine.
funFact: Ephedra is not a flowering plant: it belongs to the Gnetophytes, an odd group of gymnosperms related to conifers.

summary: A small shrub of Asian monsoon forests whose twisting roots gave medicine reserpine. It was one of the first drugs for high blood pressure and for psychosis, and its effects helped launch modern psychopharmacology.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent and Sri Lanka to Myanmar, Thailand, southern China, Malaysia and Indonesia
abilities: Roots contain over 50 indole alkaloids, including reserpine and ajmaline
Reserpine depletes the brain and nerves of noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin
White-pink flowers on red stalks are followed by glossy purple-black drupes
edibilityNote: Not a food. The root is a potent drug; self-medication is dangerous.

uses.use: Sarpagandha root for insomnia, anxiety, insanity (unmada), high blood pressure, and snake and insect bites
Asrol (root) as a sedative for hypertension, insomnia and mania
Reserpine for hypertension and formerly for psychosis; ajmaline as an antiarrhythmic and diagnostic for Brugada syndrome

medicinal.cautions: Reserpine can cause severe depression, including suicidal thoughts, as well as nasal congestion, slow heart rate, low blood pressure, stomach ulcers and parkinsonism. It interacts with MAOIs, digoxin and anaesthetics. Use only under medical supervision. Wild populations are over-collected (CITES Appendix II).

fruit.description: Small, paired, shiny purple-black drupes on red stalks.

seed.description: Single seed within a hard endocarp
seed.germination: Low and erratic (often under 50%); fresh seed sown in shade, 2–6 weeks

steps: Sow fresh seed in a shaded nursery bed at the start of the monsoon
Transplant at 2 months, 30–45 cm apart
Pinch flowers for better root growth unless saving seed
Dig roots in winter of the second year

lore: The genus honours the 16th-century German physician and botanist Leonhard Rauwolf. In 1949 the Bombay cardiologist Rustom Jal Vakil reported its blood-pressure-lowering effect in the British Heart Journal, and in 1952 chemists at Ciba isolated reserpine.
funFact: Reserpine caused depression in some patients by draining the brain of monoamines, which helped inspire the 'monoamine hypothesis' of depression.

summary: A tough little pink-and-white bedding plant from Madagascar that yields vinblastine and vincristine. These cancer drugs helped turn childhood leukaemia from almost always fatal to usually curable.
nativeRange: Endemic to Madagascar; naturalised throughout the tropics and subtropics
abilities: Makes more than 130 terpenoid indole alkaloids, including vinblastine and vincristine, which block cell division
Flowers almost continuously in warm climates
Tolerates drought, heat, salt spray and poor sandy soil
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous. Ingestion can cause low blood pressure, nerve damage and suppression of blood-cell production. Toxic to pets.

uses.use: Decoctions for diabetes, fevers, menstrual problems and as a bitter tonic
Leaf tea taken for diabetes, which led to its scientific investigation
Sadabahar leaves chewed or brewed for diabetes and wounds
Vinblastine (Hodgkin lymphoma, testicular cancer) and vincristine (acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and other cancers) as chemotherapy

medicinal.cautions: The isolated drugs are hospital chemotherapy with serious toxicity; injecting vincristine into the spine by mistake is fatal. Do not use the plant to treat diabetes or cancer: it is poisonous and its blood-sugar effect is unproven.

fruit.description: Pair of narrow, cylindrical follicles, 2–4 cm, splitting along one side.

seed.description: Small, black, grooved seeds
seed.dispersal: Gravity and ants; self-sows in warm gardens

grow.soil: Sandy, well-drained; dislikes cold wet soil
steps: Sow in warm conditions, lightly covered
Plant out after nights stay above 15 °C
Water only when dry; overwatering causes root rot
Keep away from pets and children

lore: In the 1950s Robert Noble and Charles Beer at the University of Western Ontario tested leaves sent from Jamaica as a diabetes remedy. They found no effect on blood sugar but a sharp fall in white blood cells, and isolated vinblastine. Eli Lilly separately developed vincristine.
funFact: The leaves hold only traces of vinblastine (about 1 g from 500 kg of dried leaves is often quoted), which is why chemists have long worked on making it from its more plentiful precursors, catharanthine and vindoline.

otherNames: Duǎn yè hóngdòushān 短叶红豆杉 (Chinese)
summary: A slow-growing understorey conifer of Pacific Northwest old-growth forests. Loggers once burned it as trash, until its bark yielded paclitaxel (Taxol), one of the most important cancer drugs ever found.
nativeRange: Pacific Northwest of North America, from south-east Alaska to northern California, inland to Idaho and Montana
abilities: Bark contains paclitaxel, which freezes the microtubules that dividing cells need
Tolerates deep shade beneath Douglas fir and western hemlock
Wood is extremely dense, springy and rot-resistant
Foliage and seeds contain taxine alkaloids that can stop the heart
edibilityNote: Foliage, bark and seeds are deadly poisonous (taxines). The red fleshy aril is the only non-toxic part, but the seed inside is lethal if chewed. Highly toxic to horses and cattle.

uses.use: Several nations used bark or needle preparations as medicines for various ailments and topically, and prized the wood for bows, paddles, digging sticks and tools
Paclitaxel (Taxol) for ovarian, breast and lung cancer and Kaposi sarcoma; also coats some coronary stents

medicinal.cautions: The plant is deadly: taxines cause dangerously slow and irregular heartbeat and death, sometimes without warning. Paclitaxel itself is hospital chemotherapy with serious side effects. Never prepare remedies from yew.

fruit.type: Aril (fleshy seed cup; not a true fruit)
fruit.description: Bright red, juicy cup around a single dark seed; the seed is deadly.

seed.description: Olive-brown, ovoid seed partly enclosed in a red aril
seed.dispersal: Birds swallow the arils and pass the seeds intact
seed.germination: Deeply dormant; warm then cold stratification over 1–2 years

steps: Root semi-ripe cuttings in autumn under mist, or sow seed outdoors to stratify naturally
Plant in a cool, shady, sheltered spot
Keep away from livestock and play areas
Clippings are poisonous; dispose of them carefully

lore: In 1962 USDA botanist Arthur Barclay collected Pacific yew bark in Washington for a National Cancer Institute screening programme. Monroe Wall and Mansukh Wani isolated paclitaxel in 1966 and published its structure in 1971, and the clamour for bark led to the US Pacific Yew Act of 1992.
funFact: At first the bark of several mature trees was needed to treat a single patient. The drug is now made semi-synthetically from European yew needles or by plant-cell culture.

otherNames: Zhōng yà kǔ hāo 中亚苦蒿 (Chinese)
summary: A silvery, intensely bitter perennial that gave its name to absinthe and vermouth. Its thujone was blamed for 'absinthism', and that fear got absinthe banned across much of Europe and the US in the early 20th century.
nativeRange: Temperate Europe, North Africa and Western & Central Asia; naturalised in North America
abilities: Absinthin is among the most bitter substances known in plants and stimulates bitter receptors that drive digestive secretions
Thujone blocks GABA-A receptors and can cause seizures at high doses
Releases compounds from its leaves and roots that suppress nearby plants (allelopathy)
Silky grey hairs reflect sunlight and reduce water loss
edibilityNote: Used only in tiny regulated amounts as a bitter flavouring in absinthe, vermouth and bitters. The essential oil and large doses are toxic, and the herb is not a food.

uses.use: Bitter tea or wine for poor appetite, indigestion, gallbladder complaints and intestinal worms
Afsanteen as a liver and stomach tonic, a deobstruent and for fevers and worms
EMA traditional-use monograph for loss of appetite and mild dyspepsia; a small trial in Crohn's disease

medicinal.cautions: Thujone is a convulsant: avoid the essential oil, long-term use, pregnancy, breastfeeding and epilepsy. Drinking wormwood oil has caused seizures, muscle breakdown and kidney failure. Asteraceae allergy.

fruit.description: Minute brown achenes without a pappus.

seed.description: Tiny, oblong, pale-brown seeds

grow.timeToHarvest: Leafy tops from year 2, at flowering
steps: Surface-sow under cover or root cuttings in spring
Plant away from vegetables, as its exudates inhibit neighbours
Cut flowering tops in midsummer and hang to dry
Cut back in spring to keep it compact

lore: Absinthe was banned in Switzerland (1910), the United States (1912) and France (1915). Modern analyses of pre-ban bottles found thujone levels too low to explain 'absinthism'; the high alcohol content is the more likely culprit. 'Wormwood' in English Bibles (Revelation 8:11) stands for bitterness.
funFact: The word 'vermouth' comes from the German Wermut, wormwood, the herb that gave the original fortified wines their bitterness.

otherNames: Makham pom มะขามป้อม (Thai)
summary: A feathery-leaved deciduous tree whose translucent green fruits are among the richest natural sources of vitamin C. Amla is one of the three fruits of the Ayurvedic formula Triphala and the base of the tonic jam chyawanprash.
nativeRange: Tropical and subtropical South and Southeast Asia, from India and Sri Lanka to southern China and Malaysia
abilities: Fruit is rich in vitamin C, protected from breakdown by abundant tannins
Ellagitannins and gallic acid give strong antioxidant and astringent activity
Leaves are tiny and arranged in two rows, so the shoots look like pinnate leaves
Tolerates poor, dry and somewhat saline soils
edibilityNote: Very sour and astringent raw. Widely eaten as pickles, murabba (preserve), juice and powder.

uses.use: Amalaki as a supreme rasayana for longevity, digestion, eyes, hair and skin; one of the three fruits in Triphala and the base of chyawanprash
Amla as a cold, astringent tonic for the heart, brain, stomach and hair; in Itrifal compounds
Yuganzi to clear heat, cool the blood and soothe the throat; skyu ru ra in Tibetan medicine
Small trials of extracts for cholesterol, blood sugar and dyspepsia

medicinal.cautions: Trials are small. May increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants and lower blood sugar with diabetes drugs. Large amounts can upset the stomach.

fruit.description: Round, pale yellow-green, 2–3 cm, with six faint vertical segments; translucent, sour and astringent, around a six-sided stone.

seed.description: Six small seeds inside a hard, three-chambered stone
seed.dispersal: Animals eat the fruit; deer and monkeys

grow.soil: Any well-drained soil; tolerates poor and alkaline soil
steps: Plant grafted saplings at the start of the rains, 8–10 m apart
Water through the first dry seasons
Plant two cultivars together for better fruit set
Harvest fruit when it turns translucent and pale in winter

lore: Hindus worship the amla tree on Amla Navami in the month of Kartika, when families eat meals beneath it. Chyawanprash is named after the sage Chyavana, who by legend regained his youth through it.
funFact: Its Chinese name yuganzi means 'lingering sweetness', because water drunk after eating the sour fruit tastes sweet.

summary: A deciduous tree of Asian forests whose wrinkled, tannin-rich fruit is the 'king of medicines' in Tibetan tradition. The Medicine Buddha is shown holding a sprig of it, and it is one of the three fruits of Ayurveda's Triphala.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent to Myanmar, Thailand, Indochina and south-western China
abilities: Fruit is rich in hydrolysable tannins such as chebulagic and chebulinic acid
Tannins have long been used to tan leather and, with iron, to make black dyes and inks
Laxative when ripe, astringent when unripe, an unusual dual action that Ayurveda exploits
edibleParts: fruit (as medicine: powdered, chewed or preserved)
edibilityNote: Eaten mostly as medicine. Very astringent, and laxative in larger amounts.

uses.use: Haritaki as a rasayana and gentle laxative; one of the three fruits of Triphala; for constipation, cough and wounds
A-ru-ra, the 'king of medicines', said to treat all three humours and found in a great many formulas
Halela siyah/zard in Itrifal compounds for constipation, piles, brain and digestion
Hezi as an astringent for chronic diarrhoea, dysentery and chronic cough with hoarse voice

medicinal.cautions: Can cause diarrhoea and dehydration, so avoid with acute diarrhoea or exhaustion. Traditionally avoided in pregnancy. May interact with diabetes drugs.

fruit.description: Ovoid, ridged drupe 2–4 cm, yellow-green ripening brown-black and wrinkled when dried; very astringent.

seed.description: Single seed in a hard, thick, ridged stone
seed.dispersal: Mammals such as deer and monkeys
seed.germination: Slow; crack or soak the stone; 1–3 months

grow.soil: Well-drained, including poor and stony soil
steps: Soak stones for 2–3 days, then sow in deep pots
Plant out in the rains in full sun
Protect saplings from frost and browsing
Gather fallen fruit and sun-dry

lore: The Medicine Buddha (Bhaiṣajyaguru) is traditionally painted holding a myrobalan sprig in his right hand. Medieval Arab and European pharmacies imported 'chebulic myrobalans' from India, and they were a costly drug in Renaissance Europe.
funFact: Black myrobalan (dried unripe fruit) and chebulic myrobalan (mature fruit) were sold in old apothecaries as separate drugs, though they come from the same tree.

otherNames: Xīn yè qīng niú dǎn 心叶青牛胆 (Chinese)
summary: A heart-leaved climbing vine that drapes trees across India, sending down thread-like aerial roots. Its Sanskrit name Amrita, 'nectar of immortality', reflects its toughness, and its popularity as an immune booster during COVID-19 brought both fame and safety warnings.
nativeRange: India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Nepal and Myanmar
abilities: Cut stem pieces can survive for long periods and resprout, even when hung up to dry
Sends long, thread-like aerial roots down from the canopy to the ground
Stems contain clerodane diterpenes, alkaloids such as berberine and magnoflorine, and polysaccharides studied as immune modulators
edibilityNote: Not a food. The stem is used as medicine (juice, decoction, starch 'guduchi satva').

uses.use: Guduchi as a rasayana for chronic fevers, gout, skin disease, jaundice and diabetes; the starch (satva) for burning sensations
Gilo for fevers, jaundice and as a blood purifier
Seendhil for fevers, diabetes and as a general tonic

medicinal.cautions: In 2020–21, Indian hepatologists reported cases of serious autoimmune-like liver injury after giloy use. India's AYUSH ministry suggested the culprit was the related Tinospora crispa, but investigators linked the injury to T. cordifolia itself, which is now among the most reported causes of herb-induced liver injury in India. May lower blood sugar and stimulate the immune system, so take care with diabetes, autoimmune disease or immunosuppressant drugs. Avoid in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Pea-sized, glossy red drupes in clusters.

seed.description: Curved, single seed in each drupe
seed.germination: Erratic; stem cuttings are far more reliable

steps: Plant 20–30 cm stem cuttings at the start of the rains
Give a tree, fence or trellis to climb (traditionally neem, considered best)
Water until established
Cut mature stems thicker than a finger, leaving the plant to regrow

lore: Hindu legend tells that guduchi sprang from drops of amrita that fell to earth when Indra revived the fallen monkeys of Rama's army. Ayurvedic texts hold guduchi grown on a neem tree to be the most potent.
funFact: A cut length of giloy stem left to hang on a fence can still put out fresh shoots and aerial roots, which is why it is called 'the one that never dies'.

summary: A small, thorny, gnarled desert tree of the Horn of Africa and Arabia whose bitter, aromatic resin was worth its weight in gold in antiquity. It was burned in temples, used in embalming and brought as a gift to the infant Jesus.
nativeRange: Somalia, Ethiopia, Djibouti and northern Kenya, and the southern Arabian Peninsula (Yemen, Oman, Saudi Arabia)
abilities: Bleeds a reddish oleo-gum-resin when wounded that seals the cut and deters insects and microbes
Furanosesquiterpenes in the resin have measurable antimicrobial and pain-relieving activity
Thrives in thin, stony soil on very little rain, leafing only briefly after rains
edibilityNote: Resin is used medicinally in small amounts, as incense and as a flavouring, not as food.

uses.use: Resin for wounds, stomach complaints and mouth ulcers, and burned to fumigate homes
Mur makki for wounds, chest complaints, menstrual problems and as a mouthwash
Moyao to invigorate blood and relieve pain from trauma and swelling, often with frankincense (ruxiang)
Tincture for mouth and gum inflammation; EMA traditional-use monograph

medicinal.cautions: May stimulate the uterus, so avoid in pregnancy. Can lower blood sugar and has been reported to reduce warfarin's effect. Can cause contact dermatitis. A myrrh-based drug for schistosomiasis (Mirazid) performed poorly in controlled trials.

fruit.description: Small, ovoid, pointed drupe about 7 mm long.

seed.description: Single seed within a hard stone
seed.germination: Slow and low; cuttings are more reliable

grow.soil: Stony, sandy, sharply drained, often alkaline
grow.timeToHarvest: Resin from mature trees (several years old)
steps: Root thick cuttings in dry, gritty mix in hot weather
Keep almost dry, especially when leafless
Protect from frost
Traditionally, resin is tapped by making small cuts in the bark and collecting the hardened tears weeks later

lore: Around 1470 BCE Queen Hatshepsut sent an expedition to the Land of Punt that brought back live myrrh and incense trees, as shown in reliefs at Deir el-Bahari. The Gospel of Matthew (2:11) names myrrh among the Magi's gifts.
funFact: Hatshepsut's Punt expedition is often called the first recorded attempt to transplant living trees from one country to another.

summary: A small, papery-barked tree that clings to sun-scorched limestone in Dhofar and Somalia. For thousands of years its milky resin was the backbone of the incense trade, and caravans carried it to temples from Rome to China.
nativeRange: Dhofar (southern Oman), Hadramawt (eastern Yemen) and northern Somalia
abilities: Bleeds a milky resin rich in boswellic acids, which inhibit the inflammatory enzyme 5-lipoxygenase in lab studies
Grips sheer rock with a swollen, cushion-like base
Survives in hyper-arid country by drawing on summer monsoon fog (khareef)
edibilityNote: Small pieces of high-grade resin are chewed as gum in Oman and soaked in drinking water, but it is not a food.

uses.use: Resin chewed or soaked in water for digestion, coughs and memory; smoke to purify homes and after childbirth
Kundur for memory and the brain, for coughs, diarrhoea and to heal wounds
Ruxiang to invigorate blood and relieve pain, often paired with myrrh (moyao)
Boswellia extracts (mostly the Indian B. serrata) trialled for osteoarthritis and inflammatory bowel disease

medicinal.cautions: Most clinical trials used Indian frankincense (B. serrata), not this species. It can cause stomach upset, reflux and skin rash. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy. Overtapping and grazing are reducing wild populations, so buy sustainably sourced resin.

fruit.description: Small three- to five-valved capsule.

seed.description: Small, winged seeds
seed.germination: Low; warm (25–30 °C), sharply drained gritty mix, 2–4 weeks

grow.timeToHarvest: Resin from trees about 8–10 years old
steps: Sow fresh seed in pure grit and pumice
Keep warm and barely moist
Grow in containers in a greenhouse outside desert climates
Never overwater; it is easily killed by wet roots

lore: The Land of Frankincense in Dhofar, including the ancient port of Sumhuram (Khor Rori) and the wadi Dawkah tree groves, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000. Pliny claimed southern Arabia was the richest land on earth because of the incense trade.
funFact: Its name lubān (and Greek libanos) comes from a Semitic root meaning 'white' or 'milk', after the pale resin.

summary: A woodland wildflower of eastern North America whose knotty yellow rhizome stains everything gold with berberine. Overharvesting for herbal supplements has made it a threatened species.
nativeRange: Rich deciduous forests of eastern North America, from southern Ontario to Georgia and west to Minnesota and Arkansas
abilities: Rhizome contains berberine and hydrastine, alkaloids active against many bacteria and fungi
Strongly inhibits the liver enzymes CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 in people, altering drug levels
Spreads slowly by rhizomes into clonal colonies on the forest floor
edibilityNote: Not a food. The rhizome is a bitter, potent medicine; large amounts are toxic.

uses.use: Cherokee, Iroquois and other nations used the root for eye and skin infections, sores and digestive complaints, and as a yellow dye and insect repellent
Popularised in the 19th century for catarrh, mucous membrane infections, eye washes and digestive tonics
Root products sold for colds, sore throats and digestive upset, often combined with echinacea

medicinal.cautions: Goldenseal products have little clinical evidence; berberine alone is better studied. It strongly inhibits drug metabolism and can raise levels of many medicines, including metformin and some statins, antidepressants and anticoagulants. Avoid in pregnancy, breastfeeding and in newborns, as berberine can worsen jaundice. Choose cultivated sources only.

fruit.description: Single bright red, raspberry-like cluster of fleshy berries above two leaves; not eaten.

seed.description: Small, glossy black seeds
seed.germination: Sow fresh; needs warm then cold stratification, germinating the following spring or later

grow.propagation: Rhizome division (most reliable), root cuttings or fresh seed
steps: Plant rhizome pieces with a bud 5 cm deep in autumn under hardwood shade or shade cloth
Mulch with leaf litter
Keep weeds and slugs down for several years
Harvest in autumn after the tops die back, replanting small pieces

lore: In 1997 goldenseal was listed in CITES Appendix II because of wild overharvest. The belief that it masks drugs in urine tests comes from John Uri Lloyd's 1900 novel Stringtown on the Pike, in which it fools a chemist.
funFact: Goldenseal does not hide drugs in urine tests; the myth comes from a plot device in a novel by John Uri Lloyd, who was a pharmacist and goldenseal promoter.

summary: A trailing Kalahari herb with pink trumpet flowers and a fearsome woody fruit armed with hooked arms that clamp onto animals' feet. Its secondary tubers are a major European pain remedy and an important income for San and other Kalahari harvesters.
nativeRange: Kalahari sands of Namibia, Botswana and South Africa, extending to southern Angola and Zimbabwe
abilities: Storage tubers survive the dry season and send up new stems after rain
Woody fruits with grapple hooks lodge in hooves and fur, spreading the seed widely
Tubers contain iridoid glycosides (harpagoside) with anti-inflammatory activity
edibilityNote: Not a food. The bitter dried tubers are used as tea or extract.

uses.tradition: Southern African traditional medicine (San, Khoikhoi, Tswana)
uses.use: Tuber for pain, fevers, digestive complaints and in childbirth; ointments for sores and boils
Standardised extracts for low back pain, osteoarthritis and loss of appetite; EMA traditional-use monograph

medicinal.cautions: Some trials show benefit in low back pain and osteoarthritis, but quality is limited. Causes digestive upset, and should be avoided with stomach ulcers and gallstones. May interact with warfarin, diabetes and heart-rhythm drugs. Avoid in pregnancy. Buy sustainably harvested products.

fruit.description: Hard, flattened capsule 7–20 cm across, with long arms ending in sharp hooks.

seed.description: Dark, rough, oblong seeds inside the woody fruit
seed.dispersal: Fruits hook onto the feet and fur of animals
seed.germination: Deeply dormant; erratic; needs warmth and rain

steps: Sow in deep containers of pure sand in warmth
Water in summer only and keep dry in winter
Harvest only secondary (side) tubers, leaving the central taproot
Slice and sun-dry quickly

lore: In the early 1900s G. H. Mehnert, a German settler in Namibia, learned of its use from local healers and introduced it to Europe. Today it is harvested from the wild in Namibia under community-based permit schemes.
funFact: The genus name means 'grappling-hook plant' in Greek. Its fruits can lame antelope and sheep by clamping onto their feet or mouths.

otherNames: Umckaloabo (trade name, from Zulu, roughly 'heavy cough')
summary: A low, silvery-leaved grassland pelargonium with tiny, almost black-purple flowers and a thick red tuber. A Victorian Englishman's 'tuberculosis cure' from that tuber became Germany's best-selling herbal cold remedy.
nativeRange: Highveld grasslands of South Africa and Lesotho
abilities: Tuber contains highly oxygenated coumarins such as umckalin and prodelphinidins with antimicrobial and immune-modulating activity
Thick tubers survive frost, drought and grassland fires and resprout
Flowers almost year-round in mild climates
edibilityNote: Not a food. The tuber is used as decoction or extract.

uses.tradition: Southern African traditional medicine (Sesotho, Zulu, Xhosa)
uses.use: Tuber decoction for coughs, chest infections, diarrhoea and dysentery, and for colic in calves
Root extract EPs 7630 for acute bronchitis, sinusitis and the common cold

medicinal.cautions: A Cochrane review rated the evidence that it eases bronchitis and sinusitis symptoms as low quality, and nearly all trials came from the manufacturer; the EU registers it only on the basis of traditional use. Rare cases of liver injury and allergic reactions have been reported. May theoretically increase bleeding with anticoagulants. The EU monograph restricts it to ages 6 and over; avoid in pregnancy. Wild harvesting is under pressure, so choose cultivated sources.

fruit.description: Beaked fruit splitting into five one-seeded segments with spirally twisting tails.

seed.description: Small seeds with a feathery, corkscrew tail
seed.dispersal: Wind; the tail twists with humidity and drills the seed into soil

steps: Sow seed in gritty compost in spring
Plant out in full sun with sharp drainage, or grow in pots
Water in summer and keep drier in winter
Lift tubers in autumn of year 2–3, replanting the crowns

lore: In 1897 Englishman Charles Henry Stevens travelled to South Africa for his tuberculosis. He said a Basotho healer cured him with the root, and in Britain he sold it as 'Stevens' Consumption Cure'.
funFact: Its seed tail twists and untwists with changes in humidity, working the seed into the ground like a corkscrew.
